Your own interfaces can offer the same helpers: `@FunctionalInterface` counts only abstract methods, so a `Rule` with one abstract `test` and a `default` `and` compiles, while two abstract methods are rejected ("Unexpected @FunctionalInterface annotation").

## Laziness with Supplier

A `Supplier` delays work until `get()` is called: `log.debug(() -> expensiveDump())`, `map.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> load(k))`, `optional.orElseGet(() -> fallback())` (topic 11).

The difference is measurable. On a present `Optional`, `orElse(load())` still calls `load()`, because the argument is evaluated before the call; `orElseGet(this::load)` does not call it at all. `java.util.logging.Logger.fine(Supplier<String>)` builds the message only when FINE is enabled, so with the level at INFO the supplier never runs. Pass a `Supplier` whenever the value is expensive and often unused.

## Checked exceptions do not fit

`Function.apply` declares no checked exceptions, so a lambda calling `Files.readString(path)` (which throws `IOException`) does not compile inside `map`. Options: catch inside the lambda and wrap in `UncheckedIOException`, write a small helper that wraps, or use a loop when error handling matters.

quiz.prompt: With `plus1 = x -> x + 1` and `times2 = x -> x * 2`, what is `plus1.andThen(times2).apply(3)`?
quiz.explanation: andThen runs the receiver first and the argument second: plus1 turns 3 into 4, then times2 gives 8. 7 is what compose would give, because compose runs times2 first (6) and then plus1. 6 and 5 would each apply only one of the two functions.

quiz.prompt: Which functional interface takes no arguments and returns a value?
choices: `Consumer<T>`
`Function<T, R>`
`Runnable`
`Supplier<T>`
quiz.explanation: Supplier<T> has `T get()`: no argument, one result. Consumer<T> takes a value and returns nothing, Function<T, R> takes one and returns one, and Runnable takes nothing and returns nothing, so only Supplier matches.

quiz.prompt: Why does `int count = 0; items.forEach(i -> count++);` not compile?
choices: count is reassigned, so it is not effectively final
Lambdas cannot capture local primitives such as int
count++ needs the boxed Integer type inside a lambda
It compiles, but the lambda increments a copy of count
quiz.explanation: A lambda may capture a local variable only if it is effectively final, and count++ reassigns count, so the compiler rejects it. Capturing an int is fine when it is not reassigned, boxing would not help, and Java never silently increments a copy. Count with a stream reduction such as count(), or an AtomicInteger.

quiz.prompt: What does `String::toUpperCase` stand for in `names.stream().map(String::toUpperCase)`?
choices: `() -> String.toUpperCase()`
`s -> String.toUpperCase(s)`
`s -> s.toUpperCase()`
`s -> s.toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT)`
quiz.explanation: An unbound instance-method reference calls the method on the stream element itself, so String::toUpperCase means `s -> s.toUpperCase()`, using the default locale. There is no static String.toUpperCase(s), and the reference does not add Locale.ROOT for you.

quiz.prompt: A lambda passed to `List.of(1, 2).forEach(...)` calls `Thread.sleep(10)`, and the enclosing method declares `throws InterruptedException`. Does it compile?
choices: Yes: the method's throws clause covers code inside the lambda
No: Consumer.accept declares no checked exceptions, so catch it inside
Yes, because forEach rethrows checked exceptions unchanged
No: Thread.sleep may not be called from any lambda at all
quiz.explanation: The lambda's body belongs to Consumer.accept, which declares no checked exceptions, so the enclosing method's throws clause does not help. Catch InterruptedException inside the lambda (restoring the interrupt flag) or use a plain loop.

quiz.prompt: What does `Predicate.not(String::isBlank)` give you?
choices: A predicate true for non-blank strings
A predicate true for blank strings
A Supplier<Boolean> that checks the string later
A Function<String, Boolean> that negates its input
quiz.explanation: Predicate.not wraps a predicate and negates it, so `Predicate.not(String::isBlank)` is true for strings that are NOT blank, handy in `filter`. It still returns a Predicate<String>, not a Supplier or a Function, and it does not negate the input value.

quiz.prompt: `@FunctionalInterface interface Rule { boolean test(String s); default Rule and(Rule other) { return s -> test(s) && other.test(s); } }` Does it compile?
choices: No: a functional interface cannot declare default methods
Yes: only the one abstract method counts toward the rule
No: the annotation needs exactly one method of any kind
Yes, but lambdas can no longer target Rule because of and()
quiz.explanation: @FunctionalInterface makes the compiler check that there is exactly one ABSTRACT method; default and static methods do not count. So Rule compiles and lambdas still target test, which is how Predicate itself offers and().

quiz.prompt: Which call delays an expensive fallback until it is actually needed?
choices: `optional.orElse(Objects.requireNonNull(expensive()))`
Both orElse and orElseGet defer the call
`optional.orElseGet(() -> expensive())`
Neither: both evaluate expensive() first
quiz.explanation: orElse takes a value, so Java evaluates expensive() before the call even when the Optional is present; orElseGet takes a Supplier and calls it only when the Optional is empty. Wrapping the call in requireNonNull still evaluates it first.

quiz.prompt: Why prefer `IntPredicate` over `Predicate<Integer>` in hot loops?
choices: It avoids boxing each int into an Integer object
Its test method runs across several cores at once
It caches the result for each int value it has seen
The JIT cannot inline a generic interface call
quiz.explanation: IntPredicate.test takes a primitive int, so no Integer object is created per value, while Predicate<Integer> boxes every int (outside the small cached range). It has nothing to do with running on several cores or caching results, and the JIT can inline both.

quiz.prompt: Can a lambda modify a field of an object referenced by a captured final variable?
choices: No: the captured object is frozen like the variable
Yes: only the variable itself must not be reassigned
Only in a static method, where no this is captured
Only inside a synchronized block around the lambda
quiz.explanation: Effectively final applies to the variable binding, not to the object it points to: the lambda cannot make the variable refer to another object, but it can call setters or change fields of the object it already refers to. The object is not frozen, and static methods or synchronized blocks change nothing about capture rules.

flashcards.back: Function (T to R), Predicate (T to boolean), Supplier (nothing to T), Consumer (T to nothing) and BiFunction (two arguments to R).
f.andThen(g) applies f then g; f.compose(g) applies g then f.
A local variable that is never reassigned after initialisation; only such variables may be captured by lambdas.
Static method, instance method of a particular object, instance method of the argument, and constructor.

flashcards.front: Why do checked exceptions clash with lambdas?
flashcards.back: The standard functional interfaces declare no checked exceptions, so the lambda body must catch and wrap them.

flashcards.front: What is Supplier useful for besides factories?
flashcards.back: Deferring expensive work until needed, as in lazy logging, computeIfAbsent and orElseGet.
IntPredicate, ToLongFunction and similar avoid boxing every value in performance-sensitive code.
That the interface has exactly one abstract method, so it stays usable as a lambda target.

topics.title: Streams
topics.summary: Lazy pipelines with intermediate and terminal operations, short-circuiting, single use, collectors (groupingBy, partitioningBy, toMap and its duplicate-key trap), reduce, flatMap, and Stream.toList versus Collectors.toList.
topics.lesson:
## A lazy pipeline

```java
List<String> topCustomers = orders.stream()
    .filter(o -> o.status() == Status.PAID)          // intermediate (lazy)
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Order::customer, Collectors.summingLong(Order::totalCents)))
    .entrySet().stream()
    .sorted(Map.Entry.<String, Long>comparingByValue().reversed())
    .limit(10)
    .map(Map.Entry::getKey)
    .toList();                                        // terminal: runs the pipeline
```

Intermediate operations (`filter`, `map`, `sorted`, `distinct`, `limit`) only describe work. Nothing runs until a **terminal** operation (`toList`, `collect`, `count`, `findFirst`, `anyMatch`, `forEach`). Elements flow one at a time, and short-circuiting terminals stop early: `Stream.of(1, 2, 3).filter(...).findFirst()` evaluates the filter only until the first match.

## Streams are single-use

A stream can be consumed once; calling a second terminal operation throws `IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed`. Keep the collection (or a `Supplier<Stream<T>>`) if you need to traverse twice.

This bites when a method receives a `Stream` parameter and both counts it and collects it. Laziness is also observable: in `Stream.of(1, 2, 3).filter(x -> x >= 2).findFirst()` the filter runs only twice, for 1 and 2, and never sees 3. A stream holds no data of its own, so nothing is cached between two traversals.

## Collectors you use daily

```java
Collectors.groupingBy(Order::status)                                  // Map<Status, List<Order>>
Collectors.groupingBy(Order::customer, TreeMap::new, Collectors.counting())   // sorted keys, counts
Collectors.partitioningBy(o -> o.totalCents() > 10_000)               // Map<Boolean, List<Order>>
Collectors.toMap(Order::id, o -> o)                                   // Map<Long, Order>
Collectors.joining(", ")
```

`toMap` throws `IllegalStateException: Duplicate key` when two elements map to the same key. Pass a merge function (`(a, b) -> a` or `Long::sum`) whenever keys can repeat, and a map supplier (`LinkedHashMap::new`) when order matters.

The message names the key and both values ("Duplicate key ana (attempted merging values 500 and 300)"). `toMap` also throws NullPointerException when a value is `null`, for example a nullable discount column, so map nulls to a default first. Word counts in one line: `toMap(w -> w, w -> 1, Integer::sum)` over `a, bb, a` gives `a=2` and `bb=1`.

## toList: two flavours

`stream.toList()` (Java 16+) returns an **unmodifiable** list; `collect(Collectors.toList())` returns a mutable `ArrayList` in practice (unspecified, but code relies on it). Calling `add` on the first throws `UnsupportedOperationException`.

Pick by intent. Return `stream.toList()` when callers should only read the result, which is the common case for service and controller code. Use `collect(Collectors.toCollection(ArrayList::new))` when the caller will add to the list, because that type is guaranteed, unlike `Collectors.toList()`.

## reduce and empty streams

`reduce(0, Integer::sum)` returns the identity for an empty stream. Without an identity, `reduce(Integer::sum)` returns an `Optional`; `IntStream.max()` and `average()` return `OptionalInt` / `OptionalDouble`, empty for no elements: handle "no data" explicitly.

Concretely, `Stream.<Integer>empty().reduce(0, Integer::sum)` is `0`, the same stream without an identity gives `Optional.empty`, and `IntStream.empty().average()` is `OptionalDouble.empty`. Calling `getAsDouble()` on that empty result throws `NoSuchElementException`, so an average over no orders needs a decision, not a crash.

## flatMap

`orders.stream().flatMap(o -> o.lines().stream())` turns a stream of orders into a stream of all their lines.

Each element is replaced by the elements of its stream, and the results are concatenated. `Stream.of(List.of(1, 2), List.of(3)).flatMap(List::stream).count()` is `3`; with `map` the same pipeline counts the two inner streams and gives `2`. `flatMap(Optional::stream)` keeps only the present values of a stream of `Optional`s.

## Rules of thumb

- Keep lambdas in pipelines **side-effect free**; do not add to an outside list in `forEach` when `collect` can build it.
- `sorted` is stable.
- Use `mapToLong(...).sum()` rather than boxing to `Long` for numeric totals.
- `parallelStream()` rarely helps in request handling (it uses the shared common pool) and breaks code with side effects; measure first.
- A plain loop is fine when the logic is stateful or needs checked exceptions.

quiz.prompt: When do the intermediate operations of a stream pipeline run?
choices: Immediately when called
When a terminal operation is invoked
On a background thread
When close() is called on the stream
quiz.explanation: Intermediate operations such as map and filter are lazy: they only describe the pipeline, and the terminal operation (collect, count, forEach) pulls elements through it. Nothing runs on a background thread unless you ask for a parallel stream, and close() does not execute it.

quiz.prompt: What happens when you call a second terminal operation on the same stream?
choices: It re-runs the whole pipeline from the original source
It returns the cached result of the first operation
It returns an empty result, as the stream is drained
It throws IllegalStateException: the stream is used up
quiz.explanation: A stream is single-use: after its terminal operation it is consumed, and a second terminal call throws IllegalStateException with "stream has already been operated upon or closed". It does not re-run the pipeline from the source, it caches nothing and it does not quietly return an empty result. Keep the source or a Supplier<Stream> to stream again.

quiz.prompt: `Stream.of("a", "a").collect(Collectors.toMap(s -> s, s -> 1))` does what?
choices: Throws IllegalStateException: Duplicate key
Returns {a=1}, keeping the first value
Returns {a=2}, summing the duplicate values
Throws IllegalArgumentException, as Map.of does
quiz.explanation: Collectors.toMap throws IllegalStateException ("Duplicate key a") when two elements map to the same key and no merge function is given. Pass one, as in `toMap(s -> s, s -> 1, Integer::sum)`, to keep or combine values; it never keeps the first silently.

quiz.prompt: What does `stream.toList().add(x)` do?
choices: Adds x, since Stream.toList returns a plain mutable ArrayList
Returns false and leaves the list exactly as it was before
Throws UnsupportedOperationException: it is unmodifiable
Throws IllegalStateException: the stream is already closed
quiz.explanation: Stream.toList (Java 16) returns an unmodifiable list, so add throws UnsupportedOperationException. It is not a plain ArrayList, it does not return false and leave the list alone, and the stream being closed is irrelevant once the list exists. Use collect(Collectors.toList()) or new ArrayList<>(...) when the list must change.

quiz.prompt: What does `Stream.<Integer>empty().reduce(Integer::sum)` return?
choices: `Optional.empty()`
`OptionalInt.empty()`
`null`
quiz.explanation: reduce without an identity has no sensible answer for no elements, so it returns Optional.empty() rather than 0 or null. 0 is what reduce(0, Integer::sum) would give, because the identity is the result for an empty stream. OptionalInt is what an IntStream returns, not a Stream<Integer>.

quiz.prompt: Which collector splits orders by a condition into a map that always has both a true and a false key?
choices: `partitioningBy`
`groupingBy`
`toMap`
`collectingAndThen`
quiz.explanation: partitioningBy always produces a Map<Boolean, List<T>> with both true and false keys, even when one side is empty. groupingBy by the same condition only creates keys for groups that actually occur, so a false key may be missing.

quiz.prompt: In `Stream.of(1, 2, 3).filter(...).findFirst()`, how many times does the filter run if element 2 is the first match?
quiz.explanation: Elements flow through the pipeline one at a time, and findFirst short-circuits as soon as a match comes out. The filter runs for 1 (no match) and for 2 (match), so twice; element 3 is never examined, so the answer is not 3, and 0 or 1 would mean the filter never saw element 2.

quiz.prompt: What is `Stream.of(List.of(1, 2), List.of(3)).flatMap(List::stream).count()`?
choices: It does not compile
quiz.explanation: flatMap replaces each list by the elements of its stream and concatenates them, so the stream holds 1, 2 and 3 and count is 3. With map instead of flatMap you would count the two inner streams and get 2.

quiz.prompt: Why avoid `forEach(x -> results.add(x))` into an external list?
choices: It is a side effect; collect builds the result safely
forEach is deprecated since Java 16 in favour of toList
Lambdas cannot call methods on captured local variables
forEach skips some elements whenever the stream is sorted
quiz.explanation: Adding to an external list from forEach is a side effect: the pipeline no longer says what it produces, and with a parallel stream the unsynchronised add can lose elements or throw. collect, or toList, builds the result safely in either case. forEach is not deprecated, lambdas may call methods on captured objects, and sorting never skips elements.

quiz.prompt: Is `parallelStream()` a good default inside a web request handler?
choices: Yes: each request gets its own thread pool for the stream
No: it competes for the shared common pool and rarely helps
No: a parallel stream returns List results out of order
Yes, since parallel streams use virtual threads in Java 17
quiz.explanation: parallelStream runs on the shared ForkJoinPool common pool, so every request that uses it competes for the same few threads, and the split-and-merge overhead rarely pays off for request-sized data. Requests do not get their own pool, Java 17 parallel streams do not use virtual threads, and collected results keep encounter order. Measure first.

flashcards.back: Intermediate ones such as filter and map are lazy descriptions; a terminal one such as toList or count runs the pipeline.
No. After one terminal operation it is consumed, and another throws IllegalStateException.
Without a merge function, two elements with the same key throw IllegalStateException.
The first returns an unmodifiable list; the collector returns a mutable list in practice.
With an identity it returns that value for an empty stream; without one it returns an Optional.
groupingBy groups by any key into a map of lists; partitioningBy splits into exactly two groups by a predicate.

flashcards.front: What does short-circuiting mean for streams?
flashcards.back: Operations like findFirst, anyMatch and limit stop pulling elements as soon as the answer is known.

flashcards.front: When is a plain loop better than a stream?
flashcards.back: When the logic is stateful, needs checked exceptions or early exits with complex conditions.

topics.title: Optional
topics.summary: Optional as a return type for maybe-absent values: of versus ofNullable, map, flatMap and filter chains, orElse (eager) versus orElseGet (lazy), orElseThrow, and where Optional does not belong.
topics.lesson:
## A return type that admits absence

```java
Optional<User> findByEmail(String email);   // the caller cannot forget that the user may not exist
```

`Optional` makes "no result" visible in the type. It is designed for **return values**. Do not use it for fields, method parameters or collections (return an empty list instead), and never return `null` from a method declared to return an `Optional`.

Returning `null` there compiles and does nothing at the return statement; the NullPointerException arrives later, in the caller that chains `map` or `orElse` on it. `Optional` is also not `Serializable` (`Serializable.class.isAssignableFrom(Optional.class)` is `false`), one more reason to keep it out of fields and DTOs.

## Creating

- `Optional.of(x)` when x is definitely non-null: `Optional.of(null)` throws NullPointerException.
- `Optional.ofNullable(x)` when x may be null.
- `Optional.empty()` for no value.

Choose between the first two by what you know, not by habit. `Optional.of(repoResult)` on a value that can be null turns a missing row into a NullPointerException at the wrapping line, which is exactly the crash the type was meant to prevent. Inside a service, the usual source is a map lookup or a nullable column, so `ofNullable` is the common call.

## Using without get()

```java
String city = repo.findById(id)                 // Optional<User>
    .map(User::address)                          // Optional<Address> (null result becomes empty)
    .map(Address::city)
    .filter(c -> !c.isBlank())
    .orElse("unknown");
```

- `map(f)` transforms the value if present (a null from f becomes empty).
- `flatMap(f)` is for functions that already return an Optional: `findUser(id).flatMap(u -> findManager(u.managerId()))`, avoiding `Optional<Optional<User>>`.
- `filter(p)` turns a present value that fails the test into empty.
- `ifPresent(c)` / `ifPresentOrElse(c, r)` for side effects.
- `or(() -> other)` (Java 9) tries a second Optional when the first is empty; `stream()` gives a stream of zero or one element.

Two concrete cases: `Optional.of(" ").filter(s -> !s.isBlank()).orElse("none")` returns `"none"`, because the filter empties a value that fails the test. And `Optional.of("ana").map(this::find)` with a `find` that returns `Optional<User>` gives `Optional[Optional[User[...]]]`; `flatMap` gives `Optional[User[...]]`.

## Getting the value out

| call | when empty |
|---|---|
| `orElse(x)` | returns x, but **x is always evaluated**, even when a value is present |
| `orElseGet(() -> x)` | calls the supplier only when empty |
| `orElseThrow()` | throws NoSuchElementException |
| `orElseThrow(() -> new NotFoundException(id))` | throws your exception (the usual choice in services) |
| `get()` | throws NoSuchElementException: avoid, prefer orElseThrow |

`orElse(loadDefaultFromDatabase())` runs the query on EVERY call, present or not. Use `orElseGet` for anything expensive or with side effects.

## In a service and a controller

```java
public Order getOrder(long id) {
    return orders.findById(id).orElseThrow(() -> new NotFoundException("order " + id));
}
```

The controller (or a `@ControllerAdvice`, topic 18) maps `NotFoundException` to 404, so "missing" never becomes a NullPointerException deep inside.

The repository returns `Optional`, the service decides what absence means (here: an error carrying the id), and the controller only translates that error into HTTP. A bare `orElseThrow()` would throw NoSuchElementException with the message "No value present", which tells nobody which order was missing and usually ends as a 500.

## isPresent plus get is a smell

`if (opt.isPresent()) { use(opt.get()); }` is just a null check in disguise. `opt.ifPresent(this::use)` or a `map`/`orElse` chain says the same thing without the possibility of calling `get()` on an empty Optional.

When both branches matter, `ifPresentOrElse(u -> notify(u), () -> log.warn("no user"))` replaces the `if`/`else` pair. When a value is needed, `orElseThrow(() -> new NotFoundException(id))` is the honest version of `get()`: same behaviour on a present value, a meaningful error on an empty one.

quiz.prompt: What does `Optional.of(null)` do?
choices: Returns Optional.empty()
Throws NullPointerException
Returns an Optional containing null
It fails to compile: null is not a T
quiz.explanation: Optional.of requires a non-null value and throws NullPointerException for null; use Optional.ofNullable when the value may be missing. It compiles fine, because null fits any reference type, and no Optional ever contains null.

quiz.prompt: With a value present, does `opt.orElse(expensive())` call `expensive()`?
choices: No: orElse defers its argument until the Optional is empty
No: the JIT skips the call once it sees the value is present
Yes, but its result is cached for any later orElse calls
Yes: Java evaluates the argument before orElse is called
quiz.explanation: Java evaluates method arguments before the call, so orElse(expensive()) runs expensive() even when the Optional has a value, and then ignores the result. orElse does not defer its argument, the JIT does not skip the call, and nothing is cached. orElseGet takes a Supplier and runs it only when the Optional is empty.

quiz.prompt: Which call throws a custom exception when the Optional is empty?
choices: `orElseThrow(() -> new NotFoundException(id))`
`orElseThrow(new NotFoundException(id))`
`orElseGet(() -> new NotFoundException(id))`
`ifPresentOrElse(v -> {}, () -> new NotFoundException(id))`
quiz.explanation: orElseThrow takes a Supplier of the exception, so orElseThrow(() -> new NotFoundException(id)) throws only when the Optional is empty. Passing the exception itself does not compile, orElseGet would try to return the exception as the value, and ifPresentOrElse with a Runnable that only creates the exception never throws it.

quiz.prompt: When should you use `flatMap` instead of `map` on an Optional?
choices: When the value inside the Optional is a List or a Set
Whenever the mapping function might return null
When the function itself returns an Optional
When the Optional may be empty before mapping
quiz.explanation: Use flatMap when the mapping function itself returns an Optional: map would wrap it again into Optional<Optional<T>>, while flatMap flattens it. A function that may return null is fine with map, which turns the null into an empty Optional.

quiz.prompt: What does `opt.map(f)` return when f returns null for a present value?
choices: An Optional containing null
`Optional.empty()`
`null`
The original Optional, unchanged
quiz.explanation: Optional.map wraps the function's result with ofNullable, so a null result becomes Optional.empty(). An Optional never contains null, map never returns null itself, and it does not fall back to the original value.

quiz.prompt: Where is Optional intended to be used?
choices: As method return types for maybe-absent results
As entity fields, so JPA maps nullable columns
As method parameters for optional arguments
As collection elements in place of nulls
quiz.explanation: Optional was designed as a return type for results that may be absent, so callers are forced to handle that case. As an entity field it is not mapped by JPA and is not serialisable; as a parameter it makes callers wrap arguments, where an overload is clearer; in a collection, an empty collection or a filtered list says more.

quiz.prompt: What does `Optional.of(" ").filter(s -> !s.isBlank()).orElse("none")` return?
choices: `null`
It throws
`"none"`
quiz.explanation: Optional.of(" ") holds a one-space string, and filter keeps a present value only when the predicate is true. " ".isBlank() is true, so !isBlank() is false, the Optional becomes empty and orElse returns "none". It never returns null, the original " " is filtered out, and nothing throws.

quiz.prompt: What does `Optional.empty().get()` throw?
choices: `NullPointerException`
`IllegalStateException`
`NoSuchElementException`
`UnsupportedOperationException`
quiz.explanation: get() on an empty Optional throws NoSuchElementException ("No value present"), the same exception as orElseThrow(), which says the intent explicitly and is the preferred spelling. It is not a NullPointerException, because the Optional itself is not null.

quiz.prompt: A method declared to return Optional<User> returns null. What is wrong?
choices: Callers chaining map or orElse get a NullPointerException
Nothing: the compiler wraps the returned null in Optional.empty()
It fails to compile, because null is not an Optional<User>
The JVM throws NullPointerException at the return statement
quiz.explanation: The point of Optional is that the reference itself is never null. A method that returns null where Optional<User> is declared compiles fine and nothing happens at the return; the NullPointerException comes later, in callers that chain map or orElse. The compiler never wraps null for you. Return Optional.empty() instead.

quiz.prompt: Why is `if (o.isPresent()) use(o.get());` considered a smell?
choices: It is a race: the value can vanish before get is called
It is a null check in disguise; ifPresent says it directly
get() is deprecated, so the call warns at compile time
isPresent() allocates a new Optional on every call
quiz.explanation: isPresent followed by get is a null check in disguise and invites a stray get() on an empty Optional elsewhere. ifPresent, or a map/orElse chain, says the same thing directly. There is no race, because an Optional is immutable; get is not deprecated, although orElseThrow is now the preferred name; and isPresent allocates nothing.

flashcards.back: of requires a non-null value and throws on null; ofNullable gives an empty Optional for null.
orElse evaluates its fallback every time; orElseGet calls its supplier only when the Optional is empty.
map wraps the function's plain result; flatMap is for functions that already return an Optional.
In return types of methods whose result may be missing, never in fields, parameters or collections.
repository.findById(id).orElseThrow with a supplier of a domain not-found exception.

flashcards.front: What does filter do on an Optional?
flashcards.back: Keeps a present value only if it passes the predicate; otherwise the result is empty.
It throws on an empty Optional; orElseThrow states the same failure explicitly and safely chains alternatives.

flashcards.front: Can a method returning Optional return null?
flashcards.back: It must not: callers rely on getting a non-null Optional, so return Optional.empty().

topics.title: Exceptions & try-with-resources
topics.summary: Checked versus unchecked exceptions, try-with-resources and its close order, suppressed exceptions, finally and why never to return from it, exception chaining with causes, multi-catch and translating low-level errors.
topics.lesson:
## Checked and unchecked

- **Checked** exceptions (`IOException`, `SQLException`, anything extending `Exception` but not `RuntimeException`) must be caught or declared with `throws`. They model recoverable conditions the caller should consider.
- **Unchecked** exceptions (`RuntimeException` and subclasses: `IllegalArgumentException`, `IllegalStateException`, `NullPointerException`) need no declaration. They usually signal programming errors or violated preconditions.
- **Errors** (`OutOfMemoryError`, `StackOverflowError`) are not meant to be caught.

Modern frameworks (Spring, JPA) mostly use unchecked exceptions; wrap checked ones at the boundary when the caller cannot do anything specific with them: `throw new UncheckedIOException("reading " + path, e)`.

## try-with-resources

```java
try (var conn = dataSource.getConnection();
     var stmt = conn.prepareStatement(sql)) {
    ...
}   // stmt.close() runs first, then conn.close(): reverse order of declaration
```

Anything implementing `AutoCloseable` can be declared there, and `close()` runs whether the block completes or throws. If the body throws AND `close()` also throws, the body's exception propagates and the close failure is attached as a **suppressed** exception (`e.getSuppressed()`), so the original cause is not lost. This is why try-with-resources beats a hand-written `finally { r.close(); }`, where a failing close would hide the real error.

## finally

`finally` runs after the try (and catch) on every path. Never `return` from `finally`: it overrides the try's return value and silently discards any exception being thrown:

```java
static int f() { try { return 1; } finally { return 2; } }   // returns 2
```

The exception case is worse: `try { throw new IllegalStateException("lost"); } finally { return 3; }` returns 3, and the exception disappears without a trace (javac only warns). Use `finally` for cleanup that try-with-resources cannot express, such as releasing a lock or clearing an MDC entry.

## Chaining: keep the cause

```java
try {
    return repository.load(id);
} catch (SQLException e) {
    throw new RepositoryException("loading order " + id, e);   // e becomes getCause()
}
```

Always pass the original exception as the cause. Logging frameworks print the whole chain ("Caused by: ..."), which is usually where the real answer is.

`new RuntimeException("loading order 7", new IOException("connection reset"))` prints a "Caused by: java.io.IOException: connection reset" line under its own stack trace. Copying `e.getMessage()` into the new message instead keeps the words and loses the type and the stack trace of where the failure really happened.

## Catching well

- **Multi-catch**: `catch (NumberFormatException | DateTimeParseException e)` for identical handling. The alternatives must be unrelated: `catch (IOException | FileNotFoundException e)` does not compile ("Alternatives in a multi-catch statement cannot be related by subclassing"), and the multi-catch parameter is implicitly final.
- Catch specific types, ordered from most specific to most general: a `catch (Exception e)` before `catch (IOException e)` is a compile error ("exception IOException has already been caught").
- Do not catch `Exception` to ignore it. An empty catch block turns failures into silent wrong results.
- Do not use exceptions for normal control flow (validating every row of an import by catching NumberFormatException is slow; check first or use a parse method that reports failure).

## Custom exceptions

`public class OrderNotFoundException extends RuntimeException` with a constructor taking the message (and a cause). Domain exceptions let one global handler (`@ControllerAdvice`, topic 18) map them to HTTP responses consistently.

Give the class the constructors you will use: `OrderNotFoundException(long id)` that builds the message, and one taking `(String message, Throwable cause)` for translation. Put the data the handler needs into fields (the id, not only a sentence), so the 404 body can carry it without parsing text.

quiz.prompt: Which of these is a CHECKED exception?
choices: `UncheckedIOException`
`IOException`
`IOError`
`IllegalStateException`
quiz.explanation: IOException extends Exception but not RuntimeException, so the compiler forces callers to catch it or declare it. UncheckedIOException and IllegalStateException extend RuntimeException and are unchecked, and IOError is an Error, which is unchecked too. Checked means the compiler checks the handling, not that the failure is more serious.

quiz.prompt: With `try (var a = open("a"); var b = open("b")) { ... }`, in which order are they closed?
choices: a then b, in declaration order
b then a, but only if the body throws
Only b; a must be closed by hand
b then a: last opened, first closed
quiz.explanation: Resources close in reverse order of declaration, last opened first, so b closes before a, whether the body succeeds or throws. That matters when b depends on a, such as a statement on a connection. Every declared resource is closed; none needs closing by hand.

quiz.prompt: The try body throws, and then close() also throws. What propagates?
choices: The body exception, with the close one recorded as suppressed
The close exception, and the body exception is discarded
Both, wrapped together in a new AggregateException
The body exception; the close exception is silently dropped
quiz.explanation: try-with-resources keeps the body exception as the one that propagates, because it explains what went wrong first, and records the close() failure in its getSuppressed() array. The close exception does not replace it and is not silently dropped, and Java has no AggregateException. Log getSuppressed() too when it matters.

quiz.prompt: What does `try { return 1; } finally { return 2; }` return?
choices: It does not compile
It throws
quiz.explanation: A return in finally runs after the try's return value is computed and replaces it, so the method returns 2, not 1. It compiles (with a lint warning at most) and does not throw; worse, a return in finally would even swallow an exception thrown in the try. Keep finally for cleanup only.

quiz.prompt: How do you translate an SQLException without losing it?
choices: `throw new RepositoryException("loading order: " + e.getMessage())`
`throw new RepositoryException("loading order", e)`
`log.error("loading order failed", e); return null;`
`throw new RepositoryException("loading order: " + e)`
quiz.explanation: Passing the SQLException as the cause, new RepositoryException("loading order", e), keeps its type, message and stack trace in the chain, so logs show "Caused by: java.sql.SQLException". Concatenating getMessage() or e into the text loses the stack trace, and logging then returning null hides the failure from the caller.

quiz.prompt: Which syntax handles two exception types with one block?
choices: `catch (A | B e)`
`catch (A, B e)`
`catch (A e) catch (B e)`
`catch (A && B e)`
quiz.explanation: Multi-catch uses a vertical bar between the types, `catch (A | B e)`, and e is effectively final inside. It is easy to assume a comma or && would work, but neither is valid syntax, and two catch clauses in a row are separate blocks, not one shared block.

quiz.prompt: Why is an empty `catch (Exception e) {}` dangerous?
choices: It does not compile: catch blocks cannot be empty
It rethrows the exception after the block, wrapped as unchecked
It makes every call in the try block noticeably slower
It hides every failure, so bugs become silent wrong results
quiz.explanation: An empty catch (Exception e) {} hides every failure in the try, including the bugs you did not expect, so the program carries on with wrong results and no trace. It compiles fine, it does not rethrow anything and it costs nothing at run time. Handle what you can and let the rest reach a global handler.

quiz.prompt: Which errors should application code generally NOT catch?
choices: IllegalArgumentException from input validation
IOException from file reads and network calls
Errors like OutOfMemoryError and StackOverflowError
Custom domain exceptions such as OrderNotFound
quiz.explanation: Errors such as OutOfMemoryError and StackOverflowError signal JVM-level problems the application cannot reliably recover from, so let them propagate. Validation failures, IOExceptions and domain exceptions are the expected failures that application code is meant to handle.

quiz.prompt: What can be declared in a try-with-resources header?
choices: Any object implementing AutoCloseable
Any object that declares a close() method
Only subclasses of java.io.Closeable, such as streams
Only JDBC connections, statements and result sets
quiz.explanation: The header accepts any object whose type implements AutoCloseable, and close() is then called in reverse order of declaration however the block exits. A class that merely has a close() method is not enough, Closeable is just one subinterface, and JDBC types are only the best-known examples. Implement AutoCloseable on your own resources too.

quiz.prompt: Why do Spring and JPA mostly use unchecked exceptions?
choices: Unchecked exceptions are much cheaper to throw and to catch
Callers seldom can recover, so catch-or-declare is just noise
Checked exceptions were deprecated for new APIs in Java 9
The JVM optimises unchecked exceptions into plain return codes
quiz.explanation: Most callers cannot do anything useful with a database or framework failure except let it propagate, so forcing them to catch or declare it is noise; Spring translates checked SQLExceptions into its unchecked DataAccessException tree. Unchecked exceptions are not faster, and checked ones are not deprecated.

flashcards.back: Checked ones must be caught or declared and model recoverable situations; unchecked ones extend RuntimeException and usually mean a bug or violated precondition.
Resources close in reverse order of declaration, whether the block succeeds or throws.
Failures from close calls attached to the primary exception, so the original error is not hidden by a cleanup failure.
It replaces the try's result and silently discards an exception in flight.

flashcards.front: How do you wrap an exception correctly?
flashcards.back: Throw a new, more meaningful exception and pass the original as its cause.
One catch clause listing types separated by a vertical bar, when they need identical handling.

flashcards.front: Why are domain exceptions useful in web apps?
flashcards.back: A single global handler can map each type to a consistent HTTP response.
Avoid them for expected outcomes such as invalid rows in an import; check first or use a method that reports failure.

topics.title: Dates & times with java.time
topics.summary: Instant, LocalDate, LocalDateTime, ZonedDateTime and OffsetDateTime and when to use each; immutability; month-end and DST arithmetic; Duration versus Period; parsing, formatting and the YYYY trap.
topics.lesson:
## Pick the type by what you mean

| type | means | use for |
|---|---|---|
| `Instant` | a point on the UTC timeline | timestamps: created_at, events, logs, tokens |
| `LocalDate` | a calendar date, no time zone | birthdays, due dates, business days |
| `LocalDateTime` | date and wall-clock time, no zone | rarely: it is NOT a moment in time |
| `ZonedDateTime` | date-time in a zone with its rules (`Europe/Berlin`) | scheduling in local time, DST-aware arithmetic |
| `OffsetDateTime` | date-time with a fixed offset (+02:00) | API payloads, database columns with offsets |

Store moments as `Instant` (UTC), and convert to a zone only to display or to schedule "9:00 local time". `Instant.parse("2026-11-04T23:30:00Z").atZone(ZoneId.of("Asia/Tokyo")).toLocalDate()` is already the 5th: "what day is it?" depends on the zone.

## Immutable values

```java
LocalDate d = LocalDate.of(2026, 1, 31);   // months are 1-based (unlike the old Calendar)
d.plusDays(1);                              // returns a new date; d is unchanged
d.plusMonths(1)                             // 2026-02-28: clamped to the last valid day
LocalDate.of(2024, 2, 28).plusDays(1)       // 2024-02-29 (leap year)
LocalDate.parse("2026-02-30")               // DateTimeParseException: invalid date
```

Every java.time value is immutable, so `d.plusDays(1);` on its own line does nothing: keep the result, as with `String`. Immutable values are also safe to share between threads and to use as map keys. Clamping happens per call, which makes the order of operations matter: `d.plusMonths(1).plusMonths(1)` is 2026-03-28, while `d.plusMonths(2)` is 2026-03-31. Count from the original date when the day of month must survive a short month.

## Daylight saving time

```java
var berlin = ZoneId.of("Europe/Berlin");
ZonedDateTime.of(LocalDateTime.of(2026, 3, 29, 2, 30), berlin)   // 03:30+02:00: 02:30 does not exist that night
var satNoon = ZonedDateTime.of(2026, 3, 28, 12, 0, 0, 0, berlin);
var sunNoon = ZonedDateTime.of(2026, 3, 29, 12, 0, 0, 0, berlin);
Duration.between(satNoon, sunNoon).toHours()   // 23: the clocks jumped forward that night
```

`ZonedDateTime.plusDays(1)` keeps the local time (noon to noon, 23 real hours across the spring change); `plus(Duration.ofHours(24))` adds exactly 24 hours. Choose deliberately: a daily reminder at 9:00 local wants plusDays; a 24-hour token expiry wants a Duration on an Instant.

## Duration versus Period

- `Duration`: an amount of time in seconds and nanoseconds (`Duration.ofMinutes(90)`), used with Instants.
- `Period`: years, months and days (`Period.between(jan15, mar1)` is `P1M14D`).
- `ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(a, b)` gives a plain count (45 days).

The two behave differently on a zoned value. From Saturday noon in Berlin before the spring change, `plus(Period.ofDays(1))` lands on Sunday 12:00, while `plus(Duration.ofDays(1))` lands on Sunday 13:00, exactly 24 hours later. `Duration.between` needs time-based values: on two `LocalDate`s it throws `UnsupportedTemporalTypeException`, so use `Period` or `ChronoUnit.DAYS` for dates.

## Formatting and parsing

ISO-8601 is the default for `parse` / `toString`: use it in APIs and logs. For display, `DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("dd.MM.yyyy")` (with a `Locale` for month names). The classic trap: **`YYYY` is the week-based year**, so `2026-12-31` formatted with `"YYYY-MM-dd"` prints `2027-12-31` in a US locale. Use `yyyy` (or `uuuu`).

## Testing with a Clock

Inject a `java.time.Clock` instead of calling `Instant.now()` directly; tests pass `Clock.fixed(...)` and get deterministic "now". Avoid the legacy `java.util.Date`, `Calendar` and `SimpleDateFormat` (mutable, and SimpleDateFormat is not thread-safe).

```java
Clock clock = Clock.fixed(Instant.parse("2026-03-01T10:00:00Z"), ZoneOffset.UTC);
LocalDate.now(clock)                                   // 2026-03-01
Instant.now(Clock.offset(clock, Duration.ofDays(31)))  // 2026-04-01T10:00:00Z: "a month later"
```

Every `now()` in java.time has an overload that takes a `Clock`. In production, wire `Clock.systemUTC()` as a bean; in a test, a fixed or offset clock turns "the token expires after 24 hours" into an exact assertion instead of a sleep.

quiz.prompt: Which type should a `created_at` timestamp use in Java code?
choices: `LocalDateTime`
`Instant`
`LocalDate`
`String`
quiz.explanation: Instant is a point on the UTC timeline, so it records when the row was created unambiguously, whatever the server zone. LocalDateTime has no zone or offset and is not a moment, LocalDate drops the time entirely, and a String has no ordering or arithmetic. Convert to a zone only when showing it to a person.

quiz.prompt: What is `LocalDate.of(2026, 1, 31).plusMonths(1)`?
choices: It throws
quiz.explanation: Month arithmetic in java.time keeps the date valid by clamping to the last day of the target month, so 31 January plus one month is 28 February 2026. It does not roll over into March 3, it never produces an invalid 31 February, and it does not throw.

quiz.prompt: `var d = LocalDate.of(2026, 1, 31); d.plusDays(1);` What is d afterwards?
choices: `null`
It throws
quiz.explanation: java.time values are immutable: plusDays returns a new LocalDate and leaves d unchanged, and here the result was discarded, so d is still 2026-01-31. Write `d = d.plusDays(1);`. Nothing throws and nothing becomes null.

quiz.prompt: In Europe/Berlin, how many hours are there from Saturday noon to Sunday noon on the weekend clocks go forward?
quiz.explanation: When Berlin clocks spring forward, one local hour is skipped, so Saturday noon to Sunday noon in local time is 23 real hours. 24 is the length of an ordinary day and 25 that of the autumn change, while 22 would need two skipped hours. ZonedDateTime.plusDays keeps local noon, which is why the span shrinks.

quiz.prompt: With a US default locale, what does the pattern `YYYY-MM-dd` print for 2026-12-31?
choices: It throws
quiz.explanation: YYYY is the week-based year, and with US week rules the week containing 1 January 2027 starts on Sunday 27 December 2026, so 31 December prints as 2027-12-31. It is tempting to read YYYY as the calendar year, but that is yyyy. The pattern does not throw, and the two-digit year needs yy.

quiz.prompt: What is `Period.between(2026-01-15, 2026-03-01)`?
choices: `P2M`
quiz.explanation: Period counts calendar years, months and days: from 15 January one month reaches 15 February, then 14 more days reach 1 March, so P1M14D. It is tempting to answer with the 45 that ChronoUnit.DAYS.between would give, or P2M, but hours are a Duration concept, not a Period, and two whole months have not passed.

quiz.prompt: What does `LocalDate.parse("2026-02-30")` do?
choices: Returns 2026-03-02, rolling over into March
Returns 2026-02-28, clamping to the last day
Returns null, as the date does not exist
Throws DateTimeParseException: no such date
quiz.explanation: LocalDate.parse uses ISO_LOCAL_DATE with the SMART resolver, which rejects a day that does not exist in that month, so it throws DateTimeParseException. Arithmetic such as plusMonths clamps to the last valid day; parsing never rolls over, clamps or returns null.

quiz.prompt: Why inject a `Clock` instead of calling `Instant.now()`?
choices: Instant.now() is slower than reading the time from an injected Clock
Instant.now() is deprecated in favour of Clock.instant()
Tests can pass in Clock.fixed to get deterministic time
Instant.now() is not safe to call from several threads at once
quiz.explanation: With a Clock dependency, a test passes Clock.fixed(...) and time-dependent logic becomes deterministic, without sleeping or mocking static methods. Instant.now() is neither deprecated nor unsafe across threads, and the speed difference is irrelevant.

quiz.prompt: A 24-hour API token issued at an Instant should expire when?
choices: `issued.plus(Duration.ofHours(24))`
`issued.atZone(zone).plusDays(1).toInstant()`
`LocalDateTime.now(ZoneOffset.UTC).plusDays(1)`
`LocalDate.now().plusDays(1).atStartOfDay()`
quiz.explanation: Adding a Duration to an Instant measures 24 real hours, whatever DST or time zone does. Going through a zone and plusDays(1) can give 23 or 25 hours across a DST change, and LocalDateTime or LocalDate lose the instant entirely.

quiz.prompt: Why avoid `SimpleDateFormat` in server code?
choices: It is too slow for server use, though thread-safe
It is mutable and not thread-safe when shared
It cannot parse ISO-8601 strings with an offset
It was deprecated for removal in Java 17 and later deleted
quiz.explanation: SimpleDateFormat keeps parsing state in mutable fields, so one instance shared between threads corrupts results under concurrency; it is not slow, and it is not deprecated or removed. It can parse offsets with the right pattern. java.time formatters such as DateTimeFormatter are immutable and safe to share as constants.

flashcards.back: Instant is a real moment on the UTC timeline; LocalDateTime is a wall-clock reading without a zone, not a moment.

flashcards.front: Where should time zones be applied?
flashcards.back: Store moments as UTC instants and convert to a zone only for display or for scheduling in local time.
Adding a month clamps to the last valid day, so January 31 plus one month is February 28 or 29.

flashcards.front: plusDays versus plus 24 hours across DST
flashcards.back: plusDays keeps the local clock time; adding a 24-hour Duration adds exact elapsed time.
Duration is exact seconds; Period is calendar years, months and days; ChronoUnit.between counts units.
YYYY is the week-based year and differs from the calendar year around New Year; use yyyy or uuuu.
No. Every plus or with method returns a new value; the original never changes.

flashcards.front: How do you make time-based code testable?
flashcards.back: Inject a java.time.Clock and use Clock.fixed in tests.

topics.title: Threads, executors & synchronization
topics.summary: Executors instead of raw threads, race conditions on shared counters, synchronized, AtomicInteger and ConcurrentHashMap, volatile visibility, futures and lost exceptions, deadlocks, and shutting executors down.
topics.lesson:
## Use executors, not raw threads

```java
ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4);
try {
    Future<Report> f = pool.submit(() -> buildReport(id));
    Report r = f.get(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS);   // waits; a task exception arrives wrapped in ExecutionException
} finally {
    pool.shutdown();                          // let queued tasks finish, accept no new ones
    pool.awaitTermination(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
}
```

An executor reuses a bounded set of threads and queues the rest. Always shut down the executors you create (or threads leak and the JVM may not exit). In Spring, inject a managed `TaskExecutor` instead of creating pools per request. (Virtual threads, `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()`, arrived in Java 21; they are not available on Java 17.)

An exception thrown inside a task passed to `submit` is stored in its Future: if nobody calls `get()`, it disappears silently. Call `get()`, or log inside the task.

After `shutdown()`, the pool refuses new work: a later `submit` throws `RejectedExecutionException`. A size below 1 is refused up front, because `Executors.newFixedThreadPool(0)` throws `IllegalArgumentException`. Size a pool for blocking work with arithmetic: 10 threads whose tasks each wait 100 ms on a database finish at most about 100 tasks per second, however idle the CPU is.

## Race conditions

`count++` is read, add, write: three steps. Eight threads incrementing a shared `int` 100,000 times each end up with LESS than 800,000. Shared mutable state needs coordination:

```java
synchronized (lock) { count++; }                 // mutual exclusion + visibility
AtomicInteger hits = new AtomicInteger();        // lock-free atomic operations
hits.incrementAndGet();
ConcurrentHashMap<String, Integer> counts = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
counts.merge(word, 1, Integer::sum);             // atomic per key
```

`synchronized` methods and blocks lock on a monitor: only one thread at a time runs code guarded by the same lock, and changes made inside are visible to the next thread that takes the lock.

## Visibility and volatile

Without synchronisation, one thread may never see another thread's write (CPU caches, compiler reordering). `volatile` guarantees visibility of a single variable (a `running` flag) but NOT atomicity of compound actions: `volatile int count; count++` is still a race.

The race is easy to show. Eight threads each ran `count++` 100,000 times on a `volatile int`, and on JDK 17 the totals were 250,764, 254,560 and 209,700 in three runs, far below 800,000. Use `AtomicInteger` or a lock for a counter. Keep `volatile` for a flag that one thread writes and others only read, such as a `stopRequested` field checked in a worker's loop.

## Thread-safe collections

`HashMap` and `ArrayList` are not safe for concurrent writes. Use `ConcurrentHashMap` (and its atomic `merge`, `compute`, `computeIfAbsent`), `CopyOnWriteArrayList` for read-mostly lists, or confine data to one thread. Check-then-act on a concurrent map (`if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v)`) is still a race: use `putIfAbsent` / `computeIfAbsent`.

## Deadlock

Thread 1 holds lock A and waits for B; thread 2 holds B and waits for A: both wait forever. Prevent it by always acquiring locks in the same global order, holding locks briefly, and never calling unknown code (callbacks, I/O) while holding a lock.

## Prefer not sharing

The easiest thread safety is none needed: immutable objects (records, `List.copyOf`), local variables, and message passing between tasks. In a typical Spring service, each request has its own objects; bugs come from mutable fields in singleton beans (topic 17).

`List.copyOf` takes a snapshot: adding `"b"` to the source list afterwards leaves the copy as `[a]`, and `copy.add("c")` throws `UnsupportedOperationException`. A snapshot like that can be handed to any number of tasks without a lock. A singleton bean should hold only final, injected collaborators; per-request data stays in parameters and local variables.

quiz.prompt: Eight threads each run `count++` 100,000 times on a shared int with no synchronisation. The final count is typically...
choices: Exactly 800,000, since writes to an int are always atomic
Less than 800,000: increments are lost to the race
More than 800,000, because some increments run twice
0, as each thread works on its own private copy of the int
quiz.explanation: count++ is a read, an add and a write; two threads can read the same value and both write value + 1, so increments are lost and the total ends below 800,000. Single int writes are atomic, but the whole sequence is not, and threads do share the field.

quiz.prompt: Which makes a shared counter correct under concurrency?
choices: Declaring the int field volatile
Copying it to a local variable per thread
Calling Thread.yield() before each increment
Using AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet()
quiz.explanation: AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet performs the read-modify-write as one indivisible operation (a CAS loop), so no update is lost. volatile only makes writes visible, a per-thread local copy never reaches the shared counter, and yield() changes timing, not atomicity.

quiz.prompt: What does `volatile` guarantee?
choices: Visibility of its writes to other threads, not atomicity
Atomic read-modify-write, so count++ on it is safe
Mutual exclusion, like a synchronized block around access
That its value is cached per thread for faster reads
quiz.explanation: volatile guarantees visibility: a write is seen by threads that read the field afterwards, and reads are not cached per thread. It does not make count++ atomic, because that is a read, an add and a write, and it gives no mutual exclusion like synchronized. Use it for flags; use atomics or locks for counters.

quiz.prompt: A task submitted with `submit()` throws, and nobody calls `get()`. What happens to the exception?
choices: It kills the worker thread and is printed to stderr
It is rethrown in the caller of submit()
It is captured in the Future and silently lost
It shuts down the executor after logging the failure
quiz.explanation: submit() captures the exception in the returned Future; nothing is printed and the worker thread survives, so if nobody calls get() the failure is silently lost. Call get(), handle errors inside the task, or use execute(), which does report uncaught exceptions.

quiz.prompt: What does `future.get()` throw when the task failed?
choices: The task's own exception itself, rethrown unwrapped
ExecutionException wrapping the task's exception
InterruptedException, with the task's failure as its cause
CompletionException wrapping the task's exception
quiz.explanation: Future.get() wraps the task's exception in a checked ExecutionException, so unwrap it with getCause() to see what the task threw. CompletionException is what CompletableFuture.join() uses, and InterruptedException means the waiting thread was interrupted, not that the task failed.

quiz.prompt: Why must you call `shutdown()` on an executor you created?
choices: Its non-daemon threads can keep the JVM from exiting
Otherwise queued tasks never run, since shutdown starts them
Without it, submitted tasks are cancelled when main returns
So the queue is cleared of the tasks not yet started
quiz.explanation: Executors.newFixedThreadPool and friends create non-daemon threads, which stay alive after main returns and keep the JVM from exiting until shutdown() is called. Queued tasks run without it, main returning cancels nothing, and shutdown does not clear the queue: it lets queued tasks finish, which shutdownNow does not.

quiz.prompt: Two threads take locks A then B and B then A respectively. What can happen?
choices: Nothing: the JVM detects and breaks lock cycles
Livelock, as both threads keep retrying the locks
An IllegalMonitorStateException in the second thread
Deadlock: each thread waits forever for the other
quiz.explanation: Each thread holds one lock and waits for the other's, so both can wait forever: a deadlock. The JVM does not detect or break lock cycles (a thread dump can show them), so acquire locks in one consistent order everywhere.

quiz.prompt: Is `if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v);` on a ConcurrentHashMap thread-safe?
choices: Yes: ConcurrentHashMap locks the map across both calls
Yes, as long as v is an immutable object
No: the check and the put are separate steps
Only for String keys, whose hash is cached
quiz.explanation: Each call on a ConcurrentHashMap is atomic, but containsKey followed by put is two calls, so two threads can both see the key missing and both put. The map does not lock across calls, immutable values do not change that, and String keys are no different. Use putIfAbsent or computeIfAbsent to check and insert in one step.

quiz.prompt: Each request blocks a platform thread for 200 ms while it waits on a downstream API. The executor has a fixed pool of 50 threads. What is the throughput ceiling?
choices: About 50 requests per second, one per thread
About 250 requests per second
About 10,000 requests per second, as waiting uses no CPU
No ceiling, since blocked threads are parked by the OS
quiz.explanation: Each thread finishes 5 requests per second (1 / 0.2 s), so 50 threads finish about 250; more requests queue. Blocked threads use no CPU, but they still occupy pool slots, so the pool size, not the CPU, sets the limit. Raising it costs memory per platform thread.

quiz.prompt: Where do most thread-safety bugs in Spring services come from?
choices: Local variables shared between concurrent method calls
Mutable fields in singleton beans shared across requests
Records, whose fields can be changed by other threads
Final fields assigned through constructor injection
quiz.explanation: A singleton bean serves every request concurrently, so a mutable field on it is shared state that requests overwrite. Local variables live on each call's own stack, and records and constructor-injected final fields are immutable references, so they are safe by default.

flashcards.front: Why is count++ unsafe across threads?
flashcards.back: It is a read, an add and a write; two threads can read the same value and one update is lost.
synchronized gives mutual exclusion and visibility for a block of code; AtomicInteger makes single-variable updates atomic without a lock.

flashcards.front: What does volatile do and not do?
flashcards.back: It makes writes visible to other threads but does not make compound actions such as increments atomic.

flashcards.front: Where does an exception from a submitted task go?
flashcards.back: Into its Future; get() rethrows it wrapped in ExecutionException, and if nobody calls get() it is lost.

flashcards.front: How should executors be shut down?
flashcards.back: Call shutdown, then awaitTermination, usually in a finally block, so pool threads do not leak.
Separate contains and put calls race; use putIfAbsent, computeIfAbsent or merge, which are atomic.
Acquire locks in a single consistent order, hold them briefly, and avoid calling unknown code while holding one.

flashcards.front: The simplest route to thread safety
flashcards.back: Do not share mutable state: use immutable objects, local variables and stateless singleton services.

topics.title: CompletableFuture
topics.summary: supplyAsync and the common pool, thenApply versus thenCompose versus thenCombine, allOf for fan-out, exceptionally and handle for errors, join versus get, and timeouts with orTimeout and completeOnTimeout.
topics.lesson:
## Composing asynchronous work

```java
CompletableFuture<Price> price = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> pricing.quote(sku), ioPool);
CompletableFuture<Stock> stock = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> inventory.check(sku), ioPool);

CompletableFuture<Offer> offer = price.thenCombine(stock, Offer::new)   // both results
    .thenApply(o -> o.withDiscount(rules))                              // transform
    .orTimeout(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS);                                    // fail if too slow
```

- `thenApply(f)`: transform the value (like `map`).
- `thenCompose(f)`: `f` returns another CompletableFuture; flatten it (like `flatMap`): `getUser(id).thenCompose(u -> getOrders(u))`.
- `thenCombine(other, f)`: wait for two independent futures and merge their results.
- `thenAccept` / `thenRun`: side effects at the end of a chain.

Each call returns a new stage. A plain `thenApply` runs on whichever thread completed the stage before it: on an already completed future it ran on `main`, the caller. The `...Async` variants hand the step to a pool instead. Calling `thenApply` with a function that returns a future gives a `CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<String>>`, whose `join()` yields another future rather than the value.

## Fan-out with allOf

```java
List<CompletableFuture<Quote>> futures = symbols.stream().map(s -> fetch(s)).toList();   // all started
CompletableFuture<List<Quote>> all = CompletableFuture.allOf(futures.toArray(new CompletableFuture[0]))
    .thenApply(v -> futures.stream().map(CompletableFuture::join).toList());   // join is safe: all done
```

`allOf` completes when every future is done (exceptionally if any failed); it has no results of its own, so collect them with `join` afterwards. `anyOf` completes with the first one, typed `CompletableFuture<Object>`, so its value needs a cast.

Start every call before waiting on any. In one JDK 17 run, four 100 ms calls joined one by one took 494 ms; the same four started first and awaited with `allOf` took 110 ms. When one input fails, `allOf(...).join()` throws a `CompletionException` with that failure as its cause. `allOf()` with no futures is already complete.

## Errors

- `exceptionally(e -> fallback)` recovers from a failure. It runs only on failure: `completedFuture(5).exceptionally(e -> -1).join()` is `5`, while the same handler on a failed future gives `-1`.
- `handle((value, error) -> ...)` sees both outcomes.
- `join()` rethrows a failure wrapped in unchecked `CompletionException`; `get()` wraps it in checked `ExecutionException`. Unwrap with `getCause()` before mapping errors to responses.
- A chain without an error handler that nobody joins swallows the failure silently.

The error a handler receives depends on where the failure happened. On the failed stage itself, `e` is the original `IllegalStateException`. One stage later, after a `thenApply`, it arrives wrapped in a `CompletionException`, so call `getCause()` before checking the type.

## Threads

`supplyAsync(task)` without an executor runs on `ForkJoinPool.commonPool()`, which is sized for CPU work and shared with parallel streams. Blocking I/O there can starve the whole JVM's async work: pass your own executor for I/O (`supplyAsync(task, ioPool)`).

By default the common pool has one thread fewer than there are cores: on an 8-core machine `ForkJoinPool.commonPool().getParallelism()` returned 7. Thread names show where a task ran: `ForkJoinPool.commonPool-worker-1` without an executor, `pool-1-thread-1` with a fixed pool passed in. Size an I/O pool for the calls in flight, not for the cores.

## Timeouts

- `orTimeout(d, unit)`: the future fails with `TimeoutException` if not done in time.
- `completeOnTimeout(fallback, d, unit)`: completes with a fallback value instead.

The underlying work is NOT cancelled; you only stop waiting for it.

`orTimeout` returns the same future, now failed, and `join()` throws a `CompletionException` whose cause is the `TimeoutException`. In a run with a 300 ms task and a 50 ms timeout, the task still finished and set its flag after the timeout fired. `completeOnTimeout("fallback", 50, MILLISECONDS)` on an equally slow task returned `"fallback"`.

## When to use it

Fan-out of independent remote calls (price, stock, recommendations), pipelines that must not block request threads, and integrating with async clients. For simple sequential code, plain blocking calls on virtual threads (Java 21) or a thread pool are often easier to read. Spring's `@Async` methods can return `CompletableFuture` too.

quiz.prompt: Which method chains a function that itself returns a CompletableFuture, without nesting?
choices: `thenApply`
`thenCompose`
`thenAccept`
`thenApplyAsync`
quiz.explanation: thenCompose flattens a function that returns a CompletableFuture, like flatMap, so the result is a future of the value. thenApply with that function would produce a future of a future. thenAccept consumes the value and returns a future of Void, and thenApplyAsync is thenApply on another thread, so it nests just the same.

quiz.prompt: Which method waits for two independent futures and merges their results?
choices: `thenCompose`
`allOf`
`exceptionally`
`thenCombine`
quiz.explanation: `a.thenCombine(b, (x, y) -> ...)` runs when BOTH independent futures complete and merges their results. thenCompose chains a dependent future, allOf completes with Void and no results, and exceptionally only handles failure.

quiz.prompt: What does `join()` throw when the future failed?
choices: CompletionException wrapping the cause
The original exception itself, rethrown unwrapped
ExecutionException wrapping the original cause
Nothing: it returns null for a failed future
quiz.explanation: join() throws the unchecked CompletionException, wrapping the original failure as its cause; get() throws the checked ExecutionException instead. Neither returns null for a failed future, so unwrap getCause() either way.

quiz.prompt: Which pool runs `supplyAsync(task)` when no executor is passed?
choices: A virtual thread created for each task
The thread that called supplyAsync
The shared ForkJoinPool.commonPool()
A cached thread pool shared by all futures
quiz.explanation: Without an executor, supplyAsync runs the task on ForkJoinPool.commonPool(), the pool parallel streams use too. It does not run on the calling thread, Java 17 does not create virtual threads for it, and there is no shared cached thread pool. Pass your own executor for blocking I/O so the shared pool is not starved.

quiz.prompt: What does `CompletableFuture.allOf(f1, f2)` complete with?
choices: A List of both results, in argument order
Void; join each future to read its result
The result of whichever future completes first
A Map from each future to its result
quiz.explanation: allOf returns a CompletableFuture<Void> that only signals that every input has completed; the values stay in the individual futures, so join each of them afterwards. Collecting results into a List or Map is your code's job, and anyOf is the first-wins variant.

quiz.prompt: What does `exceptionally(e -> -1)` do?
choices: Recovers a failed stage, completing it with -1
Replaces every result, success or failure, with -1
Logs the exception and then still fails the stage
Cancels the future and then completes it with -1
quiz.explanation: exceptionally runs only when the stage failed and replaces the failure with -1, so the stage completes normally; a successful value passes through unchanged. It neither logs nor cancels anything, and it does not touch successful results.

quiz.prompt: After `orTimeout(50, MILLISECONDS)` fires, is the underlying work cancelled?
choices: Yes: orTimeout interrupts the thread running the task
Yes, if the task is currently blocked on I/O
No: the future keeps waiting and the timeout is only logged
No: the future fails, but the task may keep running
quiz.explanation: orTimeout completes the future exceptionally with a TimeoutException, so waiting stops, but it does not interrupt or cancel the work, which may keep running on its thread. It is not limited to I/O and it does not merely log. Stopping the task needs a separate mechanism, such as a cancellable call or Future.cancel(true) on an executor task.

quiz.prompt: Which completes with a fallback value instead of failing on timeout?
choices: `orTimeout`
`exceptionally`
`completeOnTimeout`
`get(50, MILLISECONDS)`
quiz.explanation: completeOnTimeout(value, time, unit) completes the future with the fallback value when time runs out. orTimeout instead fails it with a TimeoutException, exceptionally only reacts to a failure, and get(timeout) throws in the caller while the future stays incomplete.

quiz.prompt: Which sees both the value and the error of a stage?
choices: `handle`
`thenApply`
`exceptionally`
`thenAccept`
quiz.explanation: handle((value, error) -> ...) runs on success and on failure and receives both, one of them null, so it can map either outcome. thenApply and thenAccept run only on success, and exceptionally only on failure.

quiz.prompt: Why is blocking I/O inside the common pool risky?
choices: Blocking calls inside the pool throw IllegalStateException
Its few shared threads block, stalling unrelated async work
The common pool rejects tasks that perform blocking I/O
Each blocked task leaks the memory of its pool thread
quiz.explanation: The common pool has about one thread per core, shared by every supplyAsync without an executor and by parallel streams. Blocking I/O parks those threads, so unrelated async work stalls. Nothing throws IllegalStateException or rejects the task, and no memory leaks; the cost is starvation. Use a dedicated executor sized for I/O.

flashcards.back: Transform a value; chain another async step that returns a future; merge the results of two independent futures.
join throws an unchecked CompletionException; get throws a checked ExecutionException. Unwrap the cause in both cases.

flashcards.front: How do you collect the results of allOf?
flashcards.back: After allOf completes, call join on each original future, which no longer blocks.

flashcards.front: Which thread pool does supplyAsync use by default?
flashcards.back: The shared ForkJoinPool common pool, which should not be blocked by I/O.
exceptionally runs only on failure to supply a fallback; handle runs on both outcomes.
orTimeout fails the future with a TimeoutException; completeOnTimeout completes it with a fallback value.

flashcards.front: Does a timeout cancel the underlying work?
flashcards.back: No; it only stops waiting, so the task may still be running.

flashcards.front: How can CompletableFuture failures go unnoticed?
flashcards.back: A chain without an error handler whose result nobody joins drops the exception silently.

topics.title: JVM memory & garbage collection
topics.summary: Heap versus stack, generational G1 collection, OutOfMemoryError versus StackOverflowError, classic memory leaks (static collections, unbounded caches, listeners), bounded caches, and the heap settings to know.
topics.lesson:
## Stack and heap

- Each thread has a **stack** of frames holding local variables and primitives; references on the stack point into the heap. Deep or infinite recursion exhausts it: `StackOverflowError`.
- **Objects** live on the shared **heap**, managed by the garbage collector. When live objects no longer fit: `OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space`.

Both are `Error`s: do not catch them to "recover"; fix the recursion or the leak.

## Generational garbage collection

Most objects die young. The heap is split into a **young generation** (new objects, collected often and cheaply) and an **old generation** (survivors, collected less often). Since Java 9 the default collector is **G1** (Garbage-First), which splits the heap into regions and aims for a pause-time target; on Java 17 you will see "G1 Young Generation" and "G1 Old Generation" collectors. ZGC and Shenandoah offer very short pauses for large heaps.

An object can be collected once nothing **reachable** refers to it. Reachability starts from GC roots: thread stacks, static fields, JNI references. That is why most Java leaks are references you forgot you were holding.

Calling `System.gc()` asks for a full collection, and on Java 17 with G1 the JVM performs one: the GC log (`-Xlog:gc`) prints a line such as `Pause Full (System.gc()) 10M->3M(34M) 16.030ms`. A call after every request therefore adds a whole-heap pause per request, while the request's short-lived objects would have died cheaply in the next young collection anyway.

## Classic leaks

- **Static collections that only grow**: `static Map<String, Session> SESSIONS` that is added to and never cleaned. Statics live as long as the class (usually the whole app).
- **Unbounded caches**: a `HashMap` cache keyed by request parameters grows until the heap is full. Bound it (size and/or time): a `LinkedHashMap` with `removeEldestEntry` for simple LRU, Caffeine in production.
- **Listeners and callbacks** registered on long-lived objects and never removed.
- **ThreadLocals** in pooled threads not cleared after each request.
- **Huge result sets**: loading a million rows into a List instead of streaming or paging.

A static field is reachable for as long as its class is loaded, so every entry put into `SESSIONS` stays reachable until code removes it. A `ThreadLocal` value belongs to the thread, not to the request: in a single-thread pool, a value set to `"user-42"` by one task was still `"user-42"` in the next task, and `null` only after `remove()`. Clear it in a `finally` block.

## Diagnosing

- `-Xmx2g` / `-Xms` set the maximum and initial heap; in containers the JVM sizes the heap from the container's memory limit (`-XX:MaxRAMPercentage` tunes it).
- `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError` writes a heap dump when OOM happens; open it in Eclipse MAT or VisualVM and look at the largest "retained size" dominators.
- `jcmd <pid> GC.heap_info`, Java Flight Recorder, and GC logs (`-Xlog:gc`) show how full the heap is and how long pauses take.

## A bounded LRU cache in a few lines

```java
static <K, V> Map<K, V> lru(int max) {
    return new LinkedHashMap<>(16, 0.75f, true) {          // true = access order
        @Override protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<K, V> eldest) { return size() > max; }
    };
}
```

With a limit of 2, putting `a` and `b`, reading `a` and then putting `c` evicts `b`, leaving the keys `[a, c]`. With `false` as the third argument (insertion order), the same steps evict `a` and leave `[b, c]`. In access order even `get` reorders the map: calling `get` inside a loop over `keySet()` throws `ConcurrentModificationException`.

It is not thread-safe: wrap it with `Collections.synchronizedMap` or use Caffeine for concurrent access.

## Reduce garbage where it matters

Streaming instead of materialising, `StringBuilder` in loops, primitive streams (`mapToLong`), and avoiding needless boxing reduce GC pressure. As always: measure first; in typical CRUD services the database dominates.

Boxing creates objects. `Long.valueOf` caches only -128 to 127, so `Long.valueOf(127) == Long.valueOf(127)` is `true` while the same test with 1000 is `false`: each boxed 1000 is a new object. `orders.stream().mapToLong(Order::cents).sum()` adds primitives, whereas `map(Order::cents).reduce(0L, Long::sum)` boxes every partial sum.

quiz.prompt: Infinite recursion in a method produces...
choices: An OutOfMemoryError once the heap is full
A StackOverflowError once the stack is full
An infinite loop that never raises an error
A JVM crash with a native core dump
quiz.explanation: Each call pushes a frame onto the thread's stack, and infinite recursion keeps pushing until the stack is exhausted, which throws StackOverflowError. The heap is not involved, so it is not an OutOfMemoryError; the error is raised rather than looping silently, and the JVM does not crash with a core dump.

quiz.prompt: Where are objects created with `new` stored?
choices: On the calling thread's stack, freed on return
In the method area, alongside the class's bytecode
In off-heap native memory, released by finalizers
On the shared heap, managed by the garbage collector
quiz.explanation: Objects created with new live on the shared heap, and the garbage collector reclaims them when nothing reaches them. The thread stack holds frames, local variables and references to those objects, not the objects, so nothing is freed on return. The method area holds class metadata, and ordinary objects are not off-heap memory freed by finalizers.

quiz.prompt: A request handler calls `System.gc()` after every request to "keep memory low". What does that do?
choices: Frees each request's objects at once, safely lowering memory use
Requests a full collection on every call, which usually makes latency worse
Nothing at all: the JVM has ignored System.gc() since Java 9
It throws unless the JVM was started with an explicit-GC flag
quiz.explanation: System.gc() asks for a full collection, and HotSpot normally performs one, so each request pays for a stop-the-world pass over the whole heap. Short-lived request objects die cheaply in the young generation anyway; forcing full collections adds pauses without reducing what is live.

quiz.prompt: Why can a `static Map` cache cause an OutOfMemoryError?
choices: Static fields live on the stack, which is much smaller
Maps over a million entries overflow their int size field
