A static stays reachable, so entries never removed pile up
Static fields are never scanned, so the GC skips their entries
quiz.explanation: Bound caches by size or time, or use a cache library. A static field lives as long as its class, which is usually the life of the app.

quiz.prompt: What does `new LinkedHashMap<>(16, 0.75f, true)` with `removeEldestEntry` returning `size() > max` give you?
choices: A thread-safe cache with atomic eviction
A size-bounded LRU cache in access order
A map sorted by key, evicting the largest
A FIFO cache that evicts by insertion order
quiz.explanation: The third constructor argument true switches LinkedHashMap to access order, so every get moves the entry to the end, and removeEldestEntry returning size() > max evicts the least recently used entry after a put: a bounded LRU cache. It is not thread-safe, it does not sort keys, and with the default false it would be FIFO by insertion.

quiz.prompt: When is an object eligible for garbage collection?
choices: When it is no longer reachable from any GC root
When the method that created it returns to its caller
When the count of references to it drops to zero
When System.gc() is called at any point after its last use
quiz.explanation: An object is eligible once no chain of references leads to it from a GC root (thread stacks, static fields, JNI handles), so cycles of unreachable objects are collected too. Java does not count references, a method returning proves nothing if a reference escaped, and System.gc() does not decide eligibility.

quiz.prompt: Which JVM flag writes a heap dump when the heap runs out?
choices: `-XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps`
`-XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError`
`-XX:+HeapDumpBeforeFullGC`
`-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError`
quiz.explanation: `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError` writes a heap dump at the moment the heap runs out; HeapDumpPath only chooses where it goes. Analyse the dump to see what retains the memory. ExitOnOutOfMemoryError exits without a dump.

quiz.prompt: Should application code catch `OutOfMemoryError` to keep going?
choices: Yes: catching it lets the JVM free memory and continue safely
No: an OutOfMemoryError cannot be caught by a catch block
No: it is an Error; fix the leak or size the heap properly
Yes, as long as the catch block logs the error first
quiz.explanation: OutOfMemoryError is an Error: catching it is possible, but after one the JVM's state may be inconsistent and the next allocation can fail again, so the right move is to fix the leak or size the heap. A catch block that logs and continues only hides the problem.

quiz.prompt: Why do most objects get collected cheaply in the young generation?
choices: Most objects die young, so little survives to be copied
Young objects are smaller, so scanning them is always cheap
The young generation is not traced; it is simply discarded
Young objects live on the thread stacks rather than on the heap
quiz.explanation: The generational hypothesis says most objects die young. A young collection copies only the few survivors and reclaims everything else wholesale, so it is fast and frees a lot of memory. Young objects are traced, not simply discarded, they are not smaller by rule, and they live on the heap, not on thread stacks.

quiz.prompt: A ThreadLocal set during a request on a pooled thread is never cleared. What can happen?
choices: Nothing: ThreadLocals are cleared when each request ends
The value leaks into later requests that reuse the thread
The value is garbage-collected along with the request object
The pooled thread throws IllegalStateException on reuse
quiz.explanation: A ThreadLocal value belongs to the thread, and pooled threads outlive requests, so a value that is never removed stays reachable and leaks into the next request served by that thread, user identity included. Nothing clears it when a request ends, it is not collected with the request object, and no exception warns you. Remove it in a finally block or a filter.

flashcards.front: Stack versus heap in the JVM
flashcards.back: Each thread's stack holds frames, primitives and references; objects live on the shared heap cleaned by the GC.
The first comes from too-deep recursion exhausting a thread's stack; the second from live objects no longer fitting in the heap.

flashcards.front: What decides whether an object can be collected?
flashcards.back: Whether it is still reachable from a GC root such as a thread stack or a static field.
Ever-growing static collections, unbounded caches, listeners never removed, and ThreadLocals left set on pooled threads.

flashcards.front: How do you build a simple LRU cache?
flashcards.back: A LinkedHashMap in access order whose removeEldestEntry returns true when the size exceeds the limit.
G1, a region-based generational collector aiming at a pause-time target.

flashcards.front: How do you investigate an OutOfMemoryError?
flashcards.back: Enable heap dumps on OOM and inspect the objects with the largest retained size in a tool like Eclipse MAT.

flashcards.front: How does the JVM size the heap in a container?
flashcards.back: From the container's memory limit, adjustable with MaxRAMPercentage, or explicitly with -Xmx.

topics.title: Spring: IoC & dependency injection
topics.summary: Beans and the application context, constructor injection, singleton and prototype scopes, resolving several candidates with @Primary, @Qualifier or List injection, circular dependencies, configuration properties and profiles.
topics.lesson:
## The container builds your object graph

```java
@Service
public class OrderService {
    private final OrderRepository orders;
    private final PaymentGateway payments;

    public OrderService(OrderRepository orders, PaymentGateway payments) {   // constructor injection
        this.orders = orders;
        this.payments = payments;
    }
}
```

Classes annotated `@Component` (or the specialisations `@Service`, `@Repository`, `@Controller`) are found by component scanning and registered as **beans**. `@Bean` methods in a `@Configuration` class register objects you construct yourself (third-party clients, configured mappers). With a single constructor, Spring injects it without `@Autowired`.

Prefer **constructor injection**: dependencies are explicit, fields can be `final`, and tests construct the class with fakes directly. Field injection (`@Autowired private Repo repo;`) hides dependencies and needs reflection to test.

## Scopes

- **singleton** (the default): one instance per application context, shared by every request and thread. Keep singleton beans **stateless**; a mutable field in a `@Service` is a concurrency bug (topic 14).
- **prototype**: a new instance every time the bean is requested.
- **request** / **session** (web apps): one per HTTP request or session.

Injecting a prototype or request-scoped bean into a singleton injects ONE instance at creation time; use `ObjectProvider<T>` (or a scoped proxy) to get fresh ones.

The drill's container shows that rule in plain Java: a singleton `Service` built from a prototype `Notifier` keeps the instance it was given, so `get(Service.class).notifier()` is the same object every time, while each `get(Notifier.class)` is new. A mutable field on a singleton is shared the same way, so concurrent requests overwrite each other's values: when request A stores `"alice"` in a `currentUser` field and request B then stores `"bob"`, A reads back `"bob"`.

## Several candidates

With two beans implementing `Notifier`, injecting a single `Notifier` fails at startup ("expected single matching bean but found 2"). Resolve it with:
- `@Primary` on the default implementation
- `@Qualifier("smsNotifier")` at the injection point (the default bean name is the class name with a lower-case first letter)
- injecting `List<Notifier>` (every bean, in order) or `Map<String, Notifier>` (by bean name), perfect for strategy and plugin patterns

A missing bean fails at startup too (`NoSuchBeanDefinitionException`), which is the point: wiring errors appear when the app starts, not on the first request.

## Circular dependencies

A needs B in its constructor and B needs A: the context cannot construct either and fails to start (Spring Boot 2.6+ rejects circular references by default). Fix the design: extract the shared logic into a third bean, or invert one dependency with an event.

## Configuration and profiles

```java
@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "payments")
public record PaymentProperties(String apiUrl, Duration timeout, int retries) {}
```

Spring Boot binds `application.properties` / `application.yml`, environment variables (`PAYMENTS_API_URL` maps to `payments.api-url` through relaxed binding) and command-line arguments, with later sources overriding earlier ones (command line wins over environment over the properties file). `@Profile("dev")` beans and `application-dev.yml` activate with `spring.profiles.active=dev`. Keep secrets out of committed files.

## Proxies: why some annotations need care

`@Transactional`, `@Cacheable` and `@Async` work by wrapping the bean in a **proxy**. Only calls that go THROUGH the proxy (from another bean) get the behaviour; a method calling another method on `this` bypasses it (topic 20).

A plain JDK proxy shows the mechanism. A `java.lang.reflect.Proxy` around an interface whose `outer()` calls `inner()` logged only `outer` when `proxy.outer()` ran, because the inner call went to the target object, not to the proxy. Calling `proxy.inner()` directly was intercepted. To get the behaviour, put the annotated method on another bean and call it through that bean.

quiz.prompt: What is the default scope of a Spring bean?
choices: `prototype`
`singleton`
`request`
`session`
quiz.explanation: Spring beans are singletons by default: one instance per application context, shared by every caller and every request. prototype, request and session scopes must be declared explicitly, which is why singleton beans must not hold per-request state.

quiz.prompt: Two beans implement `Notifier` and a class injects a single `Notifier` with no qualifier. What happens?
choices: The first bean found by classpath scanning is injected
The bean registered last overrides the first and is injected
null is injected, since the dependency is ambiguous
Startup fails: expected a single matching bean but found 2
quiz.explanation: With two candidates and no hint, Spring cannot choose, so startup fails with NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException ("expected single matching bean but found 2"). Resolve it with @Primary, @Qualifier or by injecting List<Notifier>; Spring never picks one by scan order or injects null.

quiz.prompt: How do you receive EVERY Notifier bean?
choices: Inject a List<Notifier> or Map<String, Notifier>
Call context.getBean(Notifier.class) in a loop
Mark each implementation @Primary and inject one Notifier
Inject a single Notifier; Spring merges the beans
quiz.explanation: Inject a List<Notifier> (ordered by @Order) or a Map<String, Notifier> keyed by bean name, and Spring supplies every implementation, which suits strategy and plugin patterns. Marking all of them @Primary is an error, and Spring never merges beans into one.

quiz.prompt: Why is constructor injection preferred over field injection?
choices: It avoids reflection, so the application starts faster
Field injection with @Autowired was removed in Spring 6
Dependencies are explicit and final, and tests can call new
Prototype-scoped beans cannot be injected into fields
quiz.explanation: Constructor injection makes dependencies explicit in the signature, lets the fields be final, and lets a unit test call new with fakes, no Spring needed. Field injection still works in Spring 6 and both styles use reflection at startup, so speed is not the reason, and prototype beans can be injected into fields too.

quiz.prompt: A singleton service has a mutable field holding the current user. What is the problem?
choices: None: Spring creates a new instance for every request
Concurrent requests share it and overwrite each other's user
The field leaks memory, but each request sees its own value
Spring refuses to inject a bean that has mutable fields
quiz.explanation: The singleton is shared by every concurrent request, so one request's "current user" overwrites another's and data leaks between users. Keep singletons stateless and pass the user as a parameter, or use request-scoped state. Spring does not create an instance per request.

quiz.prompt: Bean A takes B in its constructor and B takes A. What happens at startup?
choices: The context fails to start: the cycle cannot be constructed
Spring injects lazy proxies to break the cycle automatically
A is created first and receives null in place of B
It works, since Spring Boot resolves cycles by default
quiz.explanation: With constructor injection neither bean can be created first, so the context fails to start with a circular-reference error (BeanCurrentlyInCreationException). Spring does not insert lazy proxies on its own, it never passes null for a missing bean, and since Spring Boot 2.6 circular references are refused by default. Break the cycle by extracting shared logic or inverting a dependency.

quiz.prompt: Which environment variable sets `payments.api-url` in Spring Boot?
choices: `payments.api-url`
`PaymentsApiUrl`
`SPRING_PAYMENTS`
`PAYMENTS_API_URL`
quiz.explanation: Relaxed binding maps environment variables by upper-casing the property and replacing dots and dashes with underscores, so PAYMENTS_API_URL sets payments.api-url. Most shells cannot even export a name with dots and dashes, and camel-case names do not map.

quiz.prompt: A prototype-scoped bean is injected into a singleton constructor. How many prototype instances does the singleton see?
choices: A new one each time the singleton calls a method on it
None: prototype beans cannot be injected into singletons
One, created once when the singleton itself was built
One per thread that calls into the singleton's methods
quiz.explanation: Injection happens once, when the singleton is built, so the singleton keeps that one prototype instance forever. To get a fresh one each time, inject ObjectProvider<T> and call getObject(). Prototype beans can be injected; they are just not re-created per call.

quiz.prompt: Why does `@Transactional` on a method called via `this.method()` from the same class not apply?
choices: A proxy adds the behaviour, and calls on this bypass it
Spring ignores @Transactional on methods that are public
The compiler inlines this.method(), discarding its annotations
Spring rejects nested transactions, so the inner one is skipped
quiz.explanation: @Transactional works through a proxy around the bean; `this.method()` calls the target object directly and never passes through the proxy, so no transaction starts. Call it from another bean or restructure the code. Public methods are exactly the ones Spring does intercept.

quiz.prompt: What is the default name of a bean registered from `class SmsNotifier`?
choices: `com.app.SmsNotifier`
`smsNotifier`
`sms-notifier`
`notifier`
quiz.explanation: The default bean name is the simple class name with its first letter lower-cased, so class SmsNotifier is registered as smsNotifier, the name @Qualifier("smsNotifier") refers to. It is not the fully qualified class name, it is not kebab-case, and Spring does not shorten it to an interface name such as notifier.

flashcards.front: What registers a class as a Spring bean?
flashcards.back: A stereotype annotation such as @Component or @Service found by scanning, or a @Bean method in a @Configuration class.
Dependencies become visible and final, and tests can build the object directly with fakes.
Singleton: one shared instance per context. Prototype: a fresh instance every time the bean is requested.

flashcards.front: Three ways to resolve several candidate beans
flashcards.back: Mark one @Primary, name one with @Qualifier at the injection point, or inject them all as a List or Map.

flashcards.front: Why must singleton beans be stateless?
flashcards.back: One instance serves every concurrent request, so mutable per-request state in fields gets shared and overwritten.

flashcards.front: What does Spring do with circular constructor dependencies?
flashcards.back: It cannot construct the beans and fails at startup; redesign to remove the cycle.
Command-line arguments override environment variables, which override application properties files.

flashcards.front: Why do some annotations need calls from another bean?
flashcards.back: @Transactional, @Cacheable and @Async are applied by a proxy, which self-invocation through this bypasses.

topics.title: Spring Web: controllers, validation & errors
topics.summary: @RestController mappings, path variables, request params and bodies, ResponseEntity and status codes, @Valid with MethodArgumentNotValidException, @RestControllerAdvice and the most specific @ExceptionHandler, and ProblemDetail responses.

quiz.prompt: A request for `/api/orders/abc` reaches `@GetMapping("/{id}") get(@PathVariable long id)`. What status does Spring return?
quiz.explanation: The path /api/orders/abc matches the route, so it is not a 404, and GET is allowed, so not a 405. Converting "abc" to long then fails with a MethodArgumentTypeMismatchException, which Spring answers as 400 Bad Request, not as a 500 server error. A client sent a bad value, and 400 says so.

quiz.prompt: What happens when a `@Valid @RequestBody` fails validation?
choices: The method runs, and the invalid fields are null
Spring answers 500 via ConstraintViolationException
Spring answers 422 Unprocessable Entity with the error list
Spring answers 400 via MethodArgumentNotValidException
quiz.explanation: Validation runs after binding and before the controller method, so the method never runs with invalid fields. Spring throws MethodArgumentNotValidException and answers 400 listing the field errors. ConstraintViolationException belongs to method validation on other beans, not to @RequestBody, and the default status is 400, not 422.

quiz.prompt: How do you return 201 Created with a Location header?
choices: `ResponseEntity.created(uri).body(dto)`
`ResponseEntity.status(201).body(dto)`
`@ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.CREATED)`
`ResponseEntity.ok().location(uri).body(dto)`
quiz.explanation: ResponseEntity.created(uri) sets both the 201 status and the Location header, then body(dto) adds the representation. status(201) and @ResponseStatus give the status without a Location header, and ok() sends 200.

quiz.prompt: Handlers exist for `NotFoundException` and `Exception`. An `OrderNotFoundException extends NotFoundException` is thrown. Which runs?
choices: The Exception handler, since it was registered first
Both handlers, with the more specific one running first
The NotFoundException handler, as the closest type
Neither: a handler needs the exact exception type it names
quiz.explanation: Spring picks the matching @ExceptionHandler whose declared type is closest in the exception's class hierarchy, so the NotFoundException handler runs for the subclass. Only one handler runs, registration order does not decide it, and an exact type match is not required.

quiz.prompt: Why should controllers return DTOs rather than JPA entities?
choices: Jackson cannot serialise classes annotated with @Entity
Entities leak internal fields and can fail on lazy loading
DTOs serialise faster because they have no annotations
Spring MVC rejects handler methods that return entities
quiz.explanation: An entity exposes every mapped field, such as a password hash or internal flags, follows lazy associations during serialisation, and changes with the schema. Jackson can serialise @Entity classes and Spring accepts them as return values, so nothing stops you; DTOs are not faster either. Map entities to API-shaped records, which also prevents over-posting on input.

quiz.prompt: What does `@RequestParam(defaultValue = "0") int page` do when `page` is absent?
choices: Uses 0
Throws 400
Uses null
Uses 1
quiz.explanation: defaultValue = "0" makes the parameter optional and binds 0 when page is absent, so the handler gets page 0, not 1. Without defaultValue, a missing required parameter would be a 400; null is impossible for a primitive int, which is why required = false alone would fail for int.

quiz.prompt: What is ProblemDetail in Spring 6?
choices: A logging class that records failed requests
A validation annotation that describes field constraints
A MockMvc helper for asserting error responses in tests
A representation of the RFC 9457 problem-details body
quiz.explanation: ProblemDetail is Spring 6's representation of an RFC 9457 problem-details body (type, title, status, detail, instance). Return it, or throw ErrorResponseException, from @ExceptionHandler methods for consistent error responses; it is not a logger, validator or test helper.

quiz.prompt: A POST with `Content-Type: text/plain` hits a `@RequestBody` JSON endpoint. The status is...
quiz.explanation: No registered message converter can read text/plain into the DTO, so Spring answers 415 Unsupported Media Type before the method runs. 400 would mean the JSON was readable but bad, 406 is about the Accept header (what the client will take back), and 200 would need the body to be read at all.

quiz.prompt: What should a catch-all `@ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)` return to the client?
choices: A generic 500 problem body, with details only in the log
The full stack trace, so that clients can report the failure
The exception message, mapped to a 400 status
A 200 with an error flag, so clients do not retry
quiz.explanation: A catch-all handler should answer a generic 500 problem body and keep the stack trace and message in the log, so internals never leak to clients. Mapping unknown failures to 400 blames the client, and a 200 with an error flag breaks every HTTP-aware caller.

quiz.prompt: Where does the rule "SKU must be in stock" belong?
choices: In a @Positive annotation on the quantity field
In the service, reported as a 409 or 422 error
In the controller's method signature, via @Valid
In the JSON mapper, rejecting the body as it is read
quiz.explanation: Bean Validation annotations check the shape of one request; whether the SKU is in stock needs current data, so the service checks it and reports a 409 or 422. @Positive and @Valid cannot query stock, and the JSON mapper only converts types.

flashcards.front: Path variable type mismatch in Spring versus ASP.NET Core
flashcards.back: Spring matches the route, fails conversion and answers 400; an ASP.NET Core route constraint simply does not match and answers 404.

flashcards.front: What does @Valid on a @RequestBody give you?
flashcards.back: Bean Validation before the method runs, and a 400 from MethodArgumentNotValidException listing every field error.

flashcards.front: How do you send 201 with Location?
flashcards.back: Use ResponseEntity's created factory with the new resource's URI, then attach the DTO as the body.
The one declared for the exception type closest to the thrown exception in the class hierarchy.
Central exception handlers shared by all controllers, so every error maps to a consistent response.

flashcards.front: Why DTOs instead of entities in controllers?
flashcards.back: They control exactly what is exposed or accepted and avoid lazy-loading errors and over-posting.
Annotations check a request in isolation; rules needing data or state live in services and map to 409 or 422.
It only binds, validates, calls one service method and maps the result to a response.

topics.title: Spring Data JPA: entities & repositories
topics.summary: Mapping entities, the persistence context and dirty checking, what save() really does, derived query methods and @Query, relationships with mappedBy, cascade and orphanRemoval, and equals/hashCode for entities.

quiz.prompt: Inside a `@Transactional` method you load an Order and change its status. Do you need to call `save()`?
choices: Yes, or the change is discarded when the method returns
No: dirty checking writes the managed entity on commit
Yes, because modifying a loaded entity detaches it first
No, but you must call flush() yourself before returning
quiz.explanation: A loaded entity is managed by the persistence context, and dirty checking writes its changed fields at flush, which happens on commit, so no save() call is needed. Changing a field does not detach it, and you do not have to call flush() yourself.

quiz.prompt: Why are Java records unsuitable as JPA entities?
choices: Records cannot carry annotations such as @Entity or @Id
JPA forbids entity classes that override equals and hashCode
Records cannot implement Serializable, which entities need
JPA needs a no-arg constructor and a non-final, mutable class
quiz.explanation: A JPA provider instantiates entities through a no-arg constructor, sets fields after construction, and subclasses entities to build lazy proxies, so it needs a non-final, mutable class. Records are final with final fields and no no-arg constructor. They can carry annotations, override equals and implement Serializable, so those are not the reasons. Use records for DTOs and projections.

quiz.prompt: What does Spring Data generate for `countByStatus(String status)`?
choices: A count query on status, derived from the method name
Nothing: you must write the implementation of it yourself
Code that loads every row and counts them in Java
A compile error until you add an @Query annotation
quiz.explanation: Spring Data parses the method name at startup and derives a count query on status (a JPQL `select count(...) ... where status = ?`), executed in the database. No implementation or @Query is needed, and it does not load rows into Java to count them.

quiz.prompt: What does `repository.save(detached)` return for an existing entity?
choices: The same object you passed, now managed
null, since the entity already existed in the database
The managed instance produced by merge
A detached copy that the context is not tracking
quiz.explanation: For an entity that is not new, SimpleJpaRepository.save calls merge, which copies the detached object's state onto a managed instance and returns that instance. The object you passed stays detached, so it is not "now managed", the result is never null, and the returned copy is the tracked one. Keep using the returned instance from then on.

quiz.prompt: In a bidirectional Order-OrderLine relationship with `@OneToMany(mappedBy = "order")`, which side owns it?
choices: The Order side, which declares the mappedBy collection
The OrderLine side, which holds the foreign key
Both sides, each writing the foreign key
Neither, until a @JoinTable is declared
quiz.explanation: The OrderLine side owns the relationship because its table holds the foreign key; mappedBy on Order says "the other side maps this". Only changes to the owning side are written, so adding a line to order.getLines() without setting line.order stores nothing. Both sides never write the key, and no @JoinTable is needed for a foreign key.

quiz.prompt: What does `orphanRemoval = true` do?
choices: Deletes child rows removed from the parent's collection
Deletes the parent once its last child is removed
Prevents deleting a parent that still has children
Disables cascading of persist and merge to the children
quiz.explanation: With orphanRemoval = true, removing a child from the parent's collection deletes its row on flush, because a line without its order makes no sense. It does not delete the parent or block deletes, and it is separate from cascading persist and merge.

quiz.prompt: Within one persistence context, loading Order 7 twice returns...
choices: Two different objects with equal field values
A real entity first, then a proxy for it
A NonUniqueResultException on the second load
The same instance, from the first-level cache
quiz.explanation: The persistence context (the first-level cache) guarantees one Java instance per database row, so the second load returns the same object, often without a query. Two equal copies would let the same row be edited twice in one unit of work.

quiz.prompt: Why is `findByIdAndCustomerId(id, customerId)` safer than `findById(id)` in a customer-facing endpoint?
choices: It runs faster, as it can hit a composite index
It avoids lazy loading the customer association
It scopes the lookup to the caller, preventing IDOR
It caches the result per customer in the session
quiz.explanation: findByIdAndCustomerId adds the caller to the WHERE clause, so a guessed id that belongs to another customer finds nothing. That closes an insecure direct object reference (IDOR), a top API vulnerability. Speed, lazy loading and caching are not the point: the composite filter may even be slower, and nothing is cached per customer.

quiz.prompt: What is the risk of equals/hashCode based on a generated id?
choices: The id is null until persist, so the hash changes on save
Hibernate proxies report a different id than the real entity
Comparing ids is slower than comparing every field
The id changes on every merge, so equality drifts
quiz.explanation: A hash computed from the id changes when persist assigns the id, so a HashSet that received the entity before the save looks in the wrong bucket and no longer finds it. Use a natural key, or the id with a constant hashCode.

quiz.prompt: A derived query method misspells a property name. When do you find out?
choices: On the first call of that repository method
When the application context starts
Never: the query silently returns no rows
At compile time, from the annotation processor
quiz.explanation: Spring Data parses derived query names when it creates the repository, so a misspelled property makes the application context fail to start. That is long before the first call, and it is not a compile-time check: plain javac does not know about it.

flashcards.back: Changes to managed entities are detected at flush or commit and written automatically, without an explicit save.
Managed entities are tracked by an open persistence context; after the transaction ends they are detached and changes are ignored.

flashcards.front: What does save() do in Spring Data JPA?
flashcards.back: persist for a new entity, merge for an existing one; merge returns the managed instance you should keep using.
The side holding the foreign key owns the relationship; the mappedBy side is inverse, and only owning-side changes are persisted.
Cascade propagates operations such as persist and remove to children; orphanRemoval deletes children removed from the collection.
JPA needs a no-argument constructor and mutable, non-final classes for loading, tracking and lazy proxies.
Repository method names like findByStatusOrderByCreatedAtDesc are parsed into queries at startup.
Compare a stable natural key, or the id when set with a constant hashCode; avoid Lombok @Data.

topics.title: JPA transactions, lazy loading & N+1
topics.summary: @Transactional boundaries and proxies, rollback rules for checked exceptions, LazyInitializationException and open-in-view, default fetch types, the N+1 problem and its fixes (JOIN FETCH, entity graphs, batch fetching, DTO projections), and optimistic locking.
topics.lesson:
## @Transactional

```java
@Service
public class CheckoutService {
    @Transactional
    public Order checkout(long cartId) { ... }          // one transaction: all or nothing

    @Transactional(readOnly = true)
    public OrderView view(long id) { ... }              // hints the flush mode and the driver
}
```

- The annotation works through a **proxy**: only calls that come from another bean start the transaction. `this.checkout(...)` from inside the same class bypasses it (self-invocation).
- Default propagation is `REQUIRED`: join an existing transaction or start one.
- **Rollback rules**: by default only unchecked exceptions (`RuntimeException`) and `Error`s roll back. A **checked** exception thrown out of the method COMMITS the transaction unless you declare `@Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class)`. The writes made before the throw are kept: if `refund` sets an order's status to `REFUNDING` and then throws a checked `PaymentDeclinedException`, the new status is committed. Drill 2's proxy logs `begin, commit` for that case.
- Put transactions on service methods (a business operation), not on controllers or repositories one by one.

## Lazy loading and LazyInitializationException

Default fetch types: `@ManyToOne` and `@OneToOne` are **EAGER**, `@OneToMany` and `@ManyToMany` are **LAZY**. Mark `@ManyToOne` lazy explicitly (`fetch = FetchType.LAZY`) to avoid loading half the database.

A lazy association is a proxy that queries when first touched. Touching it after the persistence context closed throws `LazyInitializationException: could not initialize proxy - no Session`. Classic triggers: serialising an entity to JSON in a controller after the service transaction ended, or accessing `order.getLines()` in a background thread.

Spring Boot enables **open-in-view** by default (and logs a warning about it): the persistence context stays open until the response is written, which hides LazyInitializationException but runs lazy queries during view rendering, outside your transaction, often as N+1. Many teams set `spring.jpa.open-in-view=false` and load what each use case needs explicitly.

## The N+1 problem

```java
List<Order> orders = repo.findAll();                // 1 query
for (Order o : orders) o.getCustomer().getName();   // + 1 query per order (lazy customer)
```

Listing 200 orders this way costs 201 queries: one for the list and one per order's customer. With a batch size of 100 and 200 distinct customers it is 1 + 2 = 3. Drill 1 counts batches the same way: 1,001 distinct ids at 500 per batch is 3 calls.

Fixes:
- **JOIN FETCH**: `@Query("select o from Order o join fetch o.customer")` loads both in one query.
- **Entity graphs**: `@EntityGraph(attributePaths = "customer") List<Order> findByStatus(String s);`
- **Batch fetching**: `@BatchSize(size = 100)` or `hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size` loads lazy associations for many parents with `WHERE id IN (...)` queries: N+1 becomes 1 + N/100.
- **DTO projections**: `select new com.x.OrderRow(o.id, c.name) from Order o join o.customer c`, ideal for read endpoints.

Caveat: `join fetch` of a COLLECTION combined with pagination makes Hibernate apply the limit in memory (it warns: HHH90003004). Page the parent ids first, then fetch their children.

## Optimistic locking

A `@Version` field is checked and incremented on every update; if another transaction updated the row first, the save fails with an optimistic locking exception (`ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException` in Spring), which an API maps to **409 Conflict**.

Hibernate puts the version into the update itself: `update orders set status = ?, version = 4 where id = ? and version = 3`. When two users both loaded version 3, the first update matches one row and moves the row to version 4. The second matches 0 rows, and Hibernate turns that 0 into the exception. Reload and retry, or return 409 and let the client refresh.

## Checklist for a read endpoint

`@Transactional(readOnly = true)` service method, an explicit fetch plan (join fetch, entity graph or a DTO projection), a page size cap, and the generated SQL checked once in the logs (`spring.jpa.show-sql` or `logging.level.org.hibernate.SQL=debug`).

Cap the page size in code: `PageRequest.of(page, Math.min(size, 100))` stops `?size=100000` from loading the whole table. In the SQL log, one request should show one list query plus a fixed number of fetch queries, never one query per row.

quiz.prompt: A `@Transactional` method throws a CHECKED exception (no rollbackFor). What happens to the transaction?
choices: It rolls back, as it would for any other exception
It commits the changes made before the throw
It stays open until the caller handles it
It is retried once before rolling back
quiz.explanation: By default @Transactional rolls back only for RuntimeException and Error, so a checked exception lets the transaction commit what was written before the throw. It is easy to assume every exception rolls back, but that needs rollbackFor. The transaction does not stay open for the caller and Spring never retries it.

quiz.prompt: Method `a()` in a bean calls `this.b()`, where only `b()` is `@Transactional`. Is a transaction started for b?
choices: Yes: the annotation is honoured on any call to b()
No: a transaction needs @Transactional on the class
Yes: Spring weaves the annotation into the bytecode
No: the self-call bypasses the transactional proxy
quiz.explanation: The transaction is added by a proxy around the bean, and `this.b()` calls the target object directly, so no transaction starts for b. Move b to another bean, or put @Transactional on the entry point a(). Spring's default proxies do not weave bytecode.

quiz.prompt: What is the default fetch type of `@ManyToOne`?
choices: `EAGER`
`LAZY`
`BATCH`
`NONE`
quiz.explanation: JPA's default for @ManyToOne and @OneToOne is EAGER; collections (@OneToMany, @ManyToMany) default to LAZY. Mark to-one associations LAZY explicitly so that listing orders does not load every customer unasked. BATCH and NONE are not fetch types.

quiz.prompt: When is `LazyInitializationException` thrown?
choices: When an entity is persisted before its id has been generated
When two transactions update the same row at once
When a lazy association is read after the session closes
When a query for a single entity returns no rows
quiz.explanation: LazyInitializationException is thrown when code reads a lazy association, say order.getLines(), after the persistence context that loaded the entity has closed, so no session can run the query. It has nothing to do with id generation, concurrent updates (an optimistic locking failure) or an empty result (NoResultException). Load what you need inside the transaction or map to DTOs there.

quiz.prompt: Listing 200 orders and reading each order's lazy customer issues how many queries?
quiz.explanation: One query loads the 200 orders, and each first read of a lazy customer runs its own query, so 1 + 200 = 201: the N+1 problem. It is not 1 or 2, because nothing fetched the customers together, and not 200, because the list query counts too. A join fetch, an entity graph or batch fetching brings it down to one or two.

quiz.prompt: Which fixes the N+1 for order customers in ONE query?
choices: `select o from Order o join fetch o.customer`
`select o from Order o inner join o.customer c`
`@ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY, optional = false)`
`select o from Order o where o.customer is not null`
quiz.explanation: `join fetch` loads each order's customer in the same SELECT, which removes the N extra queries. A plain join only filters and leaves the association lazy, and changing the annotation's fetch type or filtering nulls does not change how many queries run.

quiz.prompt: What does `@BatchSize(size = 100)` on a lazy association change?
choices: Nothing, unless the association is also declared EAGER
It switches the association to eager fetching
It caps the association at 100 loaded child rows
Lazy loads are grouped into IN queries of up to 100 ids
quiz.explanation: @BatchSize keeps the association lazy, but when one proxy is initialised Hibernate loads up to 100 of them with one IN query, so N+1 becomes roughly 1 + N/100. It does not cap how many children are loaded and does not switch to eager fetching.

quiz.prompt: What is a known risk of Spring Boot's default open-in-view?
choices: It keeps one transaction open for the whole request
It disables lazy loading on every entity association
Lazy loads fire during rendering, hiding N+1 queries
It forbids @Transactional on methods in web controllers
quiz.explanation: Open-in-view keeps the persistence context open until the response is written, so lazy loads during JSON rendering succeed instead of failing, quietly running extra queries outside the service transaction and hiding N+1. It does not keep one transaction open for the request, it does not disable lazy loading, and it does not forbid @Transactional. Many teams turn it off.

quiz.prompt: Two users update the same order; it has a `@Version` field. The second commit...
choices: fails with an optimistic locking exception
overwrites the first commit without any error
merges both changes into a single new row version
waits for a row lock held by the first user
quiz.explanation: Each update checks the version it read and increments it; the second commit finds a newer version, updates zero rows and fails with an optimistic locking exception, usually mapped to 409 Conflict. It does not silently overwrite the first commit, versions are never merged into one row, and optimistic locking takes no row lock to wait on.

quiz.prompt: Why is `join fetch` of a collection plus pagination problematic?
choices: JPQL rejects join fetch combined with setMaxResults
Hibernate applies the limit in memory after loading all rows
The fetched collections arrive empty when paged
Spring Data cannot page queries that use join fetch
quiz.explanation: The SQL row limit would cut collections in half, so Hibernate loads every joined row and applies setMaxResults in memory, with a warning (HHH000104). JPQL accepts the query, the collections are complete, and Spring Data can page it; the cost is loading the whole result. Page the parent ids first, then fetch the children for that page.

flashcards.back: Unchecked exceptions and errors roll back; checked exceptions commit unless rollbackFor includes them.
It is applied by a proxy, so a method invoked through this from the same bean runs without it.
ManyToOne and OneToOne are eager; OneToMany and ManyToMany are lazy.
Touching a lazy association after its persistence context has closed, for example while serialising outside the transaction.

flashcards.front: Four fixes for N+1 in JPA
flashcards.back: join fetch, an entity graph, batch fetching with IN queries, or a DTO projection query.
Keeping the persistence context open until the response is written; it hides lazy-loading errors but runs queries outside your transaction.
Hibernate warns and paginates in memory; page the parents first, then fetch their children.
Each update checks and bumps the version; a stale update fails and should become a 409 response.

topics.title: JUnit 5 & Mockito: test behaviour, fake the boundary
topics.summary: The JUnit 5 test lifecycle and assertions, testing behaviour through the public API, Mockito stubs, default answers, argument matching and verification, spies, why to fake your own boundary instead of mocking types you do not own, and what makes a fake trustworthy.

quiz.prompt: A JUnit 5 test class has the field `List<String> seen = new ArrayList<>()`. Test A adds an item; test B asserts that `seen` is empty. What happens when both run?
choices: B fails whenever A happens to run first
B fails, because JUnit runs the methods in declaration order
B passes: each test method gets a new instance of the class
It depends on whether a @BeforeEach method clears the list
quiz.explanation: JUnit Jupiter's default lifecycle is per method: it builds a new instance of the test class for every test, so B sees a fresh empty list whichever test ran first. Declaration order plays no part and no @BeforeEach is needed to clear it. Only @TestInstance(PER_CLASS) would share the field and make B depend on A.

quiz.prompt: What does `assertThrows(IllegalArgumentException.class, () -> calc.price("SKU-1", -1))` give the test?
choices: A boolean saying whether the exception was thrown or not
The thrown exception, so its message can be checked too
Nothing; it only prints the exception's stack trace to the console
The message string, or null when nothing was thrown
quiz.explanation: assertThrows fails the test when nothing is thrown or another type is thrown. Otherwise it returns the exception, typed as IllegalArgumentException, so the next line can assert on its message. It is not a boolean check and it prints nothing; a test that only needs to know the call failed can ignore the returned value.

quiz.prompt: `List<Order> findOpen()` on a Mockito mock was never stubbed. What does a call return?
choices: null, like every other unstubbed method
It throws UnsupportedOperationException
A list that holds one mock Order
An empty list, not null
quiz.explanation: Mockito's default answer gives an empty list for a List return type, Optional.empty() for Optional, 0 or false for primitives and wrappers, and null only for other object types. An unstubbed call never throws UnsupportedOperationException and never invents a mock Order, so code that loops over the result just sees no open orders.

quiz.prompt: The test stubs `when(repo.findByEmail("ana@x.io")).thenReturn(Optional.of(ana))`. The code calls `repo.findByEmail("ANA@x.io")`. What does it get?
choices: Optional.empty(): the arguments are matched with equals
Optional.of(ana), because stubs ignore letter case
An exception, since the call matches no stub
null, because the stub has no default value
quiz.explanation: Stub arguments are compared with equals, and "ANA@x.io" is not equal to "ana@x.io", so the call matches no stub and gets the default answer for an Optional return type. Mockito never ignores letter case and does not throw or return null for an unmatched call.

quiz.prompt: Which dependency is the best candidate for a Mockito mock or a hand-written fake?
choices: A JDBC ResultSet, so that the test needs no database at all
Your own PaymentGateway interface around the card provider
The BigDecimal arithmetic inside the price calculator
The JPA EntityManager that the repository calls into
quiz.explanation: Fake the boundary you own: your PaymentGateway interface is shaped by your code, so a fake of it stays honest. Third-party types like ResultSet and EntityManager should be tested against the real thing, and plain BigDecimal arithmetic needs no double at all.

quiz.prompt: Why is mocking `EntityManager` in a repository test risky?
choices: Mockito cannot mock interfaces that come from the jakarta packages
Its methods are final, so every stub is silently ignored by Mockito
It encodes your guess of JPA, and a wrong guess still passes
The test would need a whole running Spring context
quiz.explanation: A mock of a type you do not own tests your assumptions about it, and a wrong assumption still passes. Mockito can mock jakarta interfaces and a Spring context is not needed. A repository test against a real database finds the query, mapping and flush problems the mock hides.

quiz.prompt: A test stubs five methods, calls the service, then verifies all five calls in order. What is the main problem?
choices: verify has no way to check the order in which calls happened
Five stubs make Mockito noticeably slower on every run
It mirrors the implementation, so every refactor breaks it
A stubbed method can no longer be verified
quiz.explanation: The test restates how the service works instead of what it promises, so merging or renaming two internal calls breaks it while a wrong result can still pass. Assert on the outcome and verify only the interactions that are the behaviour, such as one receipt. Speed is not the issue, and InOrder can check order when order matters.

quiz.prompt: A test writes `when(spy.loadAll()).thenReturn(List.of())` on a spy whose real `loadAll` calls the network. What happens?
choices: The stub takes effect and nothing real runs at any point
The real loadAll runs once while the stub is set up
Mockito refuses, because a spy can never be stubbed at all
The spy turns into a plain mock for every one of its methods
quiz.explanation: when(spy.loadAll()) has to call spy.loadAll() to know what to stub, and on a spy that is the real method, network call included. Mockito does not refuse to stub a spy, and the spy does not turn into a mock; doReturn(...).when(spy).loadAll() stubs without calling it.

quiz.prompt: Many tests will share a payment fake. Which behaviour should it keep from the real gateway?
choices: None: a fake should simply approve every charge it gets
A random delay on every call, so tests feel realistic
A reused idempotency key returns the first charge
A console log line for every call, to help debugging
quiz.explanation: The fake must keep the rules the code relies on. Idempotency is what makes a retry after a timeout safe, so a fake that simply approves every charge cannot test that retry. Random delays and log lines only make the tests slower and noisier.

quiz.prompt: With `MockitoExtension`'s strict stubs, a test stubs a method that the code under test never calls. What happens?
choices: The test fails with an unnecessary-stubbing error
Nothing at all: unused stubs are simply ignored
The stub carries over into the next test method
Mockito logs a warning and the test passes
quiz.explanation: MockitoExtension uses strict stubs by default, so a stub the code never calls fails the test with an unnecessary-stubbing error once the test ends. It is not simply ignored or downgraded to a warning, and it cannot carry over, because every test gets fresh mocks. An unused stub usually means the test or the code is not doing what its author thinks.

flashcards.back: By default a new instance of the test class is created for every test method, so instance fields start fresh in each test.
@BeforeEach runs before every test method; @BeforeAll runs once for the class and is a static method by default.
Unstubbed calls return null for most objects, zero or false for primitives and wrappers, and empty collections, Optional or streams for those types.

flashcards.front: How does Mockito match a stub's arguments?
flashcards.back: With equals on each argument, unless matchers are used, and then every argument of that call must be a matcher.
Stub to supply the inputs a test needs; verify only the interactions that are themselves the behaviour, such as one receipt email.

flashcards.front: Don't mock what you don't own
flashcards.back: Mock or fake your own interfaces at the boundary, and test third-party types such as JDBC or JPA against the real thing.
Use doReturn(value).when(spy).method(), because when(spy.method()) runs the real method while setting up the stub.
It keeps the real dependency's rules, such as idempotency keys and declines, so tests fail where production would fail.

topics.title: Spring Security basics: the filter chain & method security
topics.summary: How the security filter chain sits in front of every controller, first-match authorization rules and Ant patterns, the thread-local SecurityContext, how ExceptionTranslationFilter chooses 401 or 403, the ROLE_ prefix behind hasRole, proxy-based method security, and when CSRF protection applies.
topics.lesson:
## The filter chain runs before your controller

Every request passes through the servlet filters before `DispatcherServlet` picks a controller. Spring Security installs one filter, `FilterChainProxy`, which hands the request to the FIRST `SecurityFilterChain` whose matcher fits it and runs that chain's filters in order: CSRF protection, the authentication filters (bearer token, form login, HTTP Basic), `ExceptionTranslationFilter`, and `AuthorizationFilter` last. A request refused there never reaches your code.

```java
@Bean
SecurityFilterChain api(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    return http
        .securityMatcher("/api/**")
        .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
            .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.GET, "/api/health").permitAll()
            .requestMatchers("/api/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN")
            .anyRequest().authenticated())
        .oauth2ResourceServer(oauth -> oauth.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()))
        .build();
}
```

## Rules are checked in order: the first match wins

`authorizeHttpRequests` tries its rules from top to bottom and applies the first one that matches the request; later rules are never consulted. Put specific paths before general ones and `anyRequest()` last (Spring refuses a rule added after `anyRequest()`). A `/**` rule placed above `/api/admin/**` decides admin paths too. In these Ant-style patterns `*` matches exactly one path segment and `**` any number of segments, so `/api/**` also matches `/api` itself.

## Who is calling: the SecurityContext

An authentication filter that accepts the credentials stores an `Authentication` (the principal and its granted authorities) in the `SecurityContextHolder`. By default that holder is thread-local: code running on another thread, such as a plain executor or an `@Async` method, does not see the user unless the context is propagated (`DelegatingSecurityContextExecutor`). The framework clears the context when the request ends, so a pooled thread never carries one user's identity into the next request.

## 401 or 403: ExceptionTranslationFilter decides

When the authorization filter refuses a request, `ExceptionTranslationFilter` turns the exception into a response. An `AuthenticationException`, or an `AccessDeniedException` while the caller is still anonymous, starts authentication through the `AuthenticationEntryPoint`: 401 with `WWW-Authenticate` for an API, a redirect to the login page for form login. An `AccessDeniedException` for an authenticated caller goes to the `AccessDeniedHandler`: 403.

## Roles are authorities with a prefix

`hasRole("ADMIN")` checks for the granted authority `ROLE_ADMIN`; `hasAuthority("orders:write")` checks the exact string. A user granted plain `ADMIN` therefore fails every `hasRole("ADMIN")` rule. The reverse mistake is caught early: `hasRole("ROLE_ADMIN")` is refused when the chain is built, because the prefix is added for you. Pick one convention and keep it in the code that builds the authorities, for example the converter that turns a JWT's `scope` claim into `SCOPE_orders:write` authorities.

## Method security goes through a proxy

`@EnableMethodSecurity` activates `@PreAuthorize` on bean methods: `@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")`, or `@PreAuthorize("#ownerId == authentication.name")` to compare a parameter with the caller. Like `@Transactional` (topic 20) it is applied by a proxy around the bean, so a call from inside the same bean (`this.deleteAll()`) skips the check entirely.

## CSRF protection

CSRF protection is on by default in every chain that `HttpSecurity` builds: a POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE that does not carry the CSRF token is refused with 403, while GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and TRACE are left alone. It matters wherever the browser attaches the credential by itself, which is what a session cookie is. A stateless API that authenticates every request with a bearer token in the `Authorization` header does not need it, because a browser never adds that header to a cross-site request on its own; `oauth2ResourceServer` already skips the CSRF check for requests that carry a bearer token.

quiz.prompt: A request to `/api/orders` carries no credentials, and the matching rule is `authenticated()`. Where is it stopped?
choices: In the security filter chain, before any controller runs
In the controller, by an if statement on the current user
In the DispatcherServlet, while it picks a handler
At the database, when the query finds no matching user
quiz.explanation: FilterChainProxy is a servlet filter in front of DispatcherServlet, and AuthorizationFilter at the end of the chain refuses the anonymous request there, so no handler is ever picked. No if statement in your own code is involved, and no database is asked about a user: credentials that were never sent cannot be looked up.

quiz.prompt: The rules are `.requestMatchers("/**").authenticated()` and then `.requestMatchers("/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN")`. A signed-in non-admin requests `/admin/users`. What happens?
choices: 403, because the more specific admin rule takes precedence
The app fails at startup because two rules overlap
Allowed: the first matching rule, /**, decides
401, because the two rules contradict each other
quiz.explanation: authorizeHttpRequests tries its rules from top to bottom and the first match decides. /** matches /admin/users, so authenticated() lets any signed-in user through and the admin rule is never consulted. Being more specific gives no precedence, and overlapping rules do not fail startup; only a rule added after anyRequest() does. Put specific matchers first.

quiz.prompt: A user is granted the authority `ADMIN`, and the rule is `hasRole("ADMIN")`. What is the result?
choices: Allowed: hasRole and hasAuthority check the same thing
Denied: hasRole looks for the authority ROLE_ADMIN
Allowed, because the ROLE_ prefix is optional in a check
The app fails at startup: authorities need the prefix
quiz.explanation: hasRole("ADMIN") adds the ROLE_ prefix and looks for the granted authority ROLE_ADMIN, so a user holding plain ADMIN is denied. hasAuthority is the check that compares the exact string; the prefix is not optional in hasRole, and nothing fails at startup. Grant ROLE_ADMIN, or write hasAuthority("ADMIN").

quiz.prompt: An `authenticated()` rule refuses an anonymous request on an API that uses bearer tokens. What does ExceptionTranslationFilter send?
choices: 403 Forbidden, from the AccessDeniedHandler
A 302 redirect to the login page, in every case
500, because nothing handled the exception
401 with WWW-Authenticate, from the entry point
quiz.explanation: The caller is anonymous, so ExceptionTranslationFilter treats the AccessDeniedException as authentication required and calls the AuthenticationEntryPoint, not the AccessDeniedHandler that would send 403. A bearer-token resource server's entry point answers 401 with a WWW-Authenticate: Bearer challenge; a redirect to the login page is what the form-login entry point does instead.

quiz.prompt: A signed-in user lacks the role an endpoint needs. Which component answers, and with what?
choices: The AuthenticationEntryPoint, with a 401 challenge
The AccessDeniedHandler, with 403
The controller advice, with a 400 Bad Request
The CSRF filter, with a 419 status of its own
quiz.explanation: The caller is already authenticated, so signing in again would not help: ExceptionTranslationFilter passes the AccessDeniedException to the AccessDeniedHandler, which answers 403. The entry point and its 401 challenge are for anonymous callers only. A URL rule refuses the request while it is still in the security filters, so a controller advice never sees it and cannot turn it into a 400.

quiz.prompt: A service hands work to a plain thread-pool executor, and that work reads `SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication()`. What does it see?
choices: The request's user, because the context is global
No authentication: the context is thread-local by default
The user who last used that pool thread for a request
An anonymous token that the executor created for it
quiz.explanation: SecurityContextHolder keeps the context per thread by default, so the work on a pool thread sees an empty context and getAuthentication() returns null. The context is not global, and the pool thread holds no earlier request's user, because it never served a request and request threads are cleared when the request ends. Propagate the context on purpose with DelegatingSecurityContextExecutor.

quiz.prompt: `@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")` sits on `deleteAll()`. Another method of the same bean calls `this.deleteAll()` for an ordinary user. What happens?
choices: AccessDeniedException, as for any other caller
It runs: a call on this skips the security proxy
Spring rewrites the call to go through the proxy
The app fails at startup because of the self-call
quiz.explanation: @PreAuthorize is enforced by a proxy around the bean, and this.deleteAll() calls the target object directly, so the check never runs and the ordinary user deletes everything. Spring does not rewrite self-calls, nothing fails at startup, and no AccessDeniedException is thrown. Move the method to another bean when internal calls must be checked, exactly as with @Transactional.

quiz.prompt: A cookie-session app receives a form POST without the CSRF token. What is the response?
choices: 403 Forbidden: CSRF protection rejects it
200, because CSRF only applies to GET requests
401, so that the user signs in all over again
A 302 back to the form, carrying an error message
quiz.explanation: CSRF protection is on by default in every chain HttpSecurity builds and guards the state-changing methods POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE. A form POST without the token is refused with 403 Forbidden by the CSRF filter. It is not a 401, because the session itself is valid, and GET requests are exactly the ones CSRF leaves alone.

quiz.prompt: Why can a stateless API that reads a bearer token from the `Authorization` header usually disable CSRF protection?
choices: Bearer tokens are encrypted, so nobody can forge them
A browser never adds that header to a cross-site request
CSRF only applies to HTML forms, never to JSON bodies
Spring checks the Origin header of every API call anyway
quiz.explanation: CSRF abuses credentials the browser attaches automatically, such as cookies. A header the page's own code must add cannot be sent by a forged cross-site form. Bearer tokens are not safe because they are encrypted, and CSRF is not limited to HTML forms: JSON endpoints with cookie sessions need it too.

quiz.prompt: Two SecurityFilterChain beans exist: one with `securityMatcher("/api/**")`, ordered first, and one with no matcher. How is a request to `/api/orders` handled?
choices: Both chains run, one after the other
The chain with no matcher always takes precedence
Only the first chain whose matcher fits it
Spring merges the two chains' rules into one list
quiz.explanation: FilterChainProxy picks exactly one SecurityFilterChain per request: the first, in order, whose matcher fits. /api/orders matches the API chain, so its filters alone run and the chain with no matcher is never consulted. Chains are not merged and do not run one after the other; the catch-all chain only handles what the earlier ones did not match.

flashcards.back: An ordered list of security filters for the requests its matcher selects; FilterChainProxy runs the first matching chain before the servlet.

flashcards.front: How does authorizeHttpRequests pick a rule?
flashcards.back: In declaration order: the earliest rule that fits the path and method wins, so specific paths go first and anyRequest() goes last.
hasRole("X") prepends the ROLE_ prefix before comparing; hasAuthority("X") compares the string exactly as it was granted.

flashcards.front: Where does the current user live?
flashcards.back: In the SecurityContextHolder. Its default strategy keeps one context per thread, and the framework clears it when the request ends.
The AuthenticationEntryPoint starts authentication (401 or a login redirect); the AccessDeniedHandler refuses a known caller (403).

flashcards.front: Access denied for an anonymous caller
flashcards.back: ExceptionTranslationFilter treats it as "authentication required" and calls the entry point rather than the access-denied handler.
@EnableMethodSecurity plus @PreAuthorize on bean methods, enforced by a proxy, so a call on this inside the bean is not checked.
On for state-changing requests with cookie sessions: a POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE without the token is refused.

topics.title: Jackson: JSON contracts that survive change
topics.summary: How Jackson names JSON keys, unknown properties in plain Jackson versus Spring Boot, absent versus null versus defaults, dates and money on the wire, enums that evolve, why entities are the wrong contract, and which contract changes old readers and old writers survive.
topics.lesson:
## The JSON is a contract, not your class

```java
public record OrderResponse(
    @JsonProperty("id") String id,
    @JsonProperty("total") BigDecimal total,
    @JsonInclude(JsonInclude.Include.NON_NULL) String note,
    Instant createdAt) {}
```

Jackson builds the JSON keys from the Java names it finds: public getters and fields, and the components of a record (bound through its canonical constructor since Jackson 2.12). Rename the Java field `total` to `amount` and the wire key changes with it, so every client that reads `total` breaks at once. `@JsonProperty` pins the external name and lets the Java name change freely. Treat the response and request DTOs as published API: separate classes from your entities, reviewed like any other interface.

## Unknown properties: strict by default, tolerant in Spring Boot

A plain `new ObjectMapper()` has `DeserializationFeature.FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES` on: a body with a key the class does not declare throws `UnrecognizedPropertyException`. Spring Boot's auto-configured mapper turns that feature off, so the same key is skipped without a word. Tolerance lets servers add response fields without breaking clients (the tolerant reader). It also means a misspelled field in a request, `emial`, is silently dropped, so a PATCH that matters should check its keys on purpose.

## Missing, null and the default value

A key that is absent leaves a field at its Java default: `null` for objects, `0` or `false` for primitives. An explicit `null` for an `int` also becomes `0` unless `FAIL_ON_NULL_FOR_PRIMITIVES` is on. So a body without `quantity` binds to `quantity == 0` with no error; use `Integer` plus validation when "not sent" must be refused. A DTO field cannot tell `{}` from `{"phone": null}` either: both leave `null`. A PATCH that must clear some fields and keep others reads the body as a `Map` or `JsonNode` and asks `containsKey`. On the way out, `@JsonInclude(NON_NULL)` drops null fields, so readers must treat a missing key and a null value alike.

## Dates, money and numbers

`java.time` types need the `JavaTimeModule`; Spring Boot registers it and turns off `WRITE_DATES_AS_TIMESTAMPS`, so an `Instant` goes out as an ISO-8601 string such as `"2026-03-07T10:00:00Z"`. A bare `ObjectMapper` with the module writes a number of seconds instead. Money as a JSON number with decimals is risky: many clients parse every number as a binary double, and Jackson itself reads a decimal into a `double` when the target is untyped (a `Map` or `Object`) unless `USE_BIG_DECIMAL_FOR_FLOATS` is set. Send amounts as integer minor units (`"totalCents": 1999`) or as a decimal string with its currency.

## Enums evolve too

An enum is written as its `name()`. Reading a value the enum does not have, say a new `"REFUNDED"` status, throws `InvalidFormatException` by default, in plain Jackson and in Spring Boot alike. Renaming a constant is a breaking change on the wire. Clients that must survive new values mark a fallback constant with `@JsonEnumDefaultValue` and enable `READ_UNKNOWN_ENUM_VALUES_USING_DEFAULT_VALUE`.

## Never serialize entities

An entity is the wrong contract: it exposes columns such as `passwordHash`, it changes whenever the schema does, and its relations fight the serializer. A bidirectional `Order` / `OrderLine` pair recurses order, lines, order, until Jackson fails with an infinite-recursion error, and a lazy collection either fires extra queries while the response is written (open-in-view) or, with open-in-view off, throws `LazyInitializationException` (topic 20). Map entities to DTOs inside the service.

## Change a contract in a way old clients survive

Ask who reads and who writes. For a response, adding an optional field is safe for tolerant readers; removing or renaming a field that was always present, changing its type, or letting it go missing breaks them. For a request, a new required field breaks every old client that does not send it, while a new optional field does not. Expand first (add the new name, keep the old), migrate the clients, then contract.

quiz.prompt: A plain `new ObjectMapper()` reads `{"id": 7, "nickname": "x"}` into a class that declares only `id`. What happens?
choices: nickname is skipped and id is read as 7
It throws UnrecognizedPropertyException
nickname is stored in a hidden map on the object
id is read and nickname becomes a null field
quiz.explanation: A bare ObjectMapper has FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES on, so a key the class does not declare stops the read with an exception. Skipping the key silently is what Spring Boot's auto-configured mapper does, because it turns that feature off. Jackson never invents a field or a hidden map unless the class asks for one with @JsonAnySetter.

quiz.prompt: A PATCH body in a Spring Boot app arrives as `{"emial": "ana@new.io"}`, a typo for `email`. With the default mapper and a DTO, what happens?
choices: The request fails with a 400 for the unknown key
Spring maps it to email by the closest field name
The server returns 500 because the bind fails
The key is skipped and the email does not change
quiz.explanation: Spring Boot's mapper disables FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES, so the misspelled key is dropped without a word and the handler sees an empty patch. That tolerance helps clients survive new response fields, but on a PATCH it hides mistakes; nothing guesses the closest name. Check the keys on purpose when a silent no-op would hurt.

quiz.prompt: A request body omits `quantity`, and the DTO declares `int quantity`. What does the bound object hold?
choices: 0, with no error: the field keeps its default
null, until a validator rejects the missing value
The bind fails with a missing-property error
-1, which Jackson uses for missing numbers
quiz.explanation: An absent key is never written, so the primitive keeps its Java default of 0, and Jackson raises no missing-property error by default. An int cannot hold null, so @NotNull cannot catch it either. Declare Integer and validate it when not sending a quantity must be refused instead of meaning zero.

quiz.prompt: A developer renames the DTO record component `total` to `amount`. There is no annotation. What do existing clients see?
choices: Nothing changes: Jackson keeps the old key name
Jackson writes both total and amount for one release
The key becomes amount; readers of total break
The app fails at startup until a mapping is added
quiz.explanation: Jackson derives the wire name from the Java name, so the rename quietly changes the contract and every client that reads total gets nothing. No release writes both keys and nothing fails at startup. Pin the external name with @JsonProperty("total"), or expand and contract: add amount, keep total until the clients move.

quiz.prompt: In a Spring Boot app, a response DTO has an `Instant createdAt`. What does the JSON hold?
choices: A number of milliseconds since the epoch, as a long
An ISO-8601 string such as "2026-03-07T10:00:00Z"
An object with seconds and nanos fields
Nothing, because Jackson cannot write Instant
quiz.explanation: Spring Boot registers the JavaTimeModule and turns off WRITE_DATES_AS_TIMESTAMPS, so an Instant goes out as an ISO-8601 string. A bare ObjectMapper with the module writes a numeric timestamp instead, and one without the module refuses java.time types. The output never becomes an object of seconds and nanos.

quiz.prompt: The server adds the status `REFUNDED`. A Java client whose `Status` enum lacks it reads a refunded order with default settings. What happens?
choices: status is set to null and the read goes on
The read succeeds with the first enum constant
The unknown value is kept as a plain string
The read fails with InvalidFormatException
quiz.explanation: Jackson refuses an enum value it cannot map, by default in plain Jackson and in Spring Boot. Reading it as null needs READ_UNKNOWN_ENUM_VALUES_AS_NULL, and a fallback constant needs @JsonEnumDefaultValue plus its feature. A new enum value is therefore a breaking change for strict clients, just like a removed field.

quiz.prompt: A controller returns an `Order` entity whose `lines` each point back to their `order`. There are no Jackson annotations. What happens when the response is written?
choices: Jackson writes each order once and skips the cycle
It recurses order, lines, order until it fails
The lines are left out because they are lazy
Spring converts the entity to a DTO on its own
quiz.explanation: Jackson follows every getter, so order leads to lines, each line back to order, and the recursion ends in an infinite-recursion error. It does not detect the cycle by itself, and Spring never converts entities to DTOs. Map to a DTO inside the service; @JsonManagedReference and @JsonBackReference only patch the symptom.

quiz.prompt: A PATCH DTO has a `String phone` field. How can the handler tell `{}` (keep the phone) from `{"phone": null}` (clear it)?
choices: Check whether phone is null after binding
Mark the field @JsonInclude(NON_NULL)
It cannot: both leave phone null
Jackson sets phone to an empty string for null
quiz.explanation: An absent key and an explicit null both leave the field null, so a null check cannot separate keep from clear. @JsonInclude affects writing, not reading, and Jackson never swaps null for an empty string. Read the body as a Map or JsonNode and ask containsKey, or use a wrapper type that records whether a field was sent.

quiz.prompt: Why send a price as integer cents (`"totalCents": 1999`) or a decimal string rather than `"total": 19.99`?
choices: Many clients parse JSON numbers as doubles
JSON has no syntax for numbers with a decimal point
Jackson cannot write a BigDecimal as a JSON number
Integers make the response body much smaller
quiz.explanation: JSON can carry 19.99, and Jackson writes BigDecimal as a number, but many readers, including JavaScript and a Jackson read into a double field or an untyped Map, turn it into a binary float that cannot hold most cents exactly. Size is not the issue. Integer minor units or a decimal string keep the amount exact on every client.

quiz.prompt: A response DTO marks `note` with `@JsonInclude(Include.NON_NULL)`, and the order has no note. What does a client receive?
choices: note set to the empty string
"note": null in the object
The note key is left out of the object
An error, because note is required
quiz.explanation: NON_NULL drops a property whose value is null, so the object has no note key at all rather than "note": null or an empty string. Nothing fails, because the annotation only shapes output. Clients must then treat a missing key and a null value the same way, which is worth saying in the API docs.

flashcards.front: Where do Jackson's JSON key names come from?
flashcards.back: From the Java names it finds: public getters and fields and record components. @JsonProperty pins an external name so the Java name can change.

flashcards.front: FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES, plain Jackson versus Spring Boot
flashcards.back: A bare ObjectMapper turns an undeclared key into an error; Spring Boot's mapper switches the feature off and skips such keys.
A client that ignores keys it does not know, so a server can add response fields without a coordinated release.

flashcards.front: Absent key versus explicit null in a DTO
flashcards.back: Both leave an object field null; a PATCH that must tell them apart reads a Map or JsonNode and checks containsKey.
Boot registers the JavaTimeModule and writes dates as ISO-8601 strings, not numeric timestamps.
Integer minor units or a decimal string plus currency, never a float that every client may parse as a binary double.

flashcards.front: A new enum value on the server
flashcards.back: Breaking for strict readers; a client survives it with @JsonEnumDefaultValue and the matching read feature, or by reading the value as text.
Safe: add an optional response field, add an optional request field. Unsafe: remove, rename or retype a field, or add a required request field.

topics.title: Bean Validation in depth: null rules, cascading, groups, errors
topics.summary: Where constraints live and when they run, NotNull versus NotEmpty versus NotBlank, why null passes every other constraint, @Valid cascading into nested objects and list elements, method validation through a proxy, custom and cross-field constraints, groups and Default, and a 400 body that helps without leaking secrets.

quiz.prompt: A DTO has `@Size(min = 2, max = 40) String name`. The request body has no `name` at all. What does validation report?
choices: A size violation, since null has no length
Nothing: Size treats null as valid
A NullPointerException inside the validator
A 500, because the field could not be bound
quiz.explanation: Every built-in constraint except the NotNull family treats null as valid, so Size has nothing to check and the request passes. That is deliberate: each annotation checks one property. A required name needs @NotBlank or @NotNull next to @Size; the validator neither throws nor turns a missing field into a size violation.

quiz.prompt: Which constraint refuses `null`, `""` and `"   "` for a String field?
choices: @NotNull
@NotEmpty
@Size(min = 1)
@NotBlank
quiz.explanation: @NotBlank refuses null and any string whose trimmed content is empty. @NotEmpty refuses null and the empty string but accepts three spaces, @NotNull accepts both empty forms, and @Size(min = 1) passes null and counts spaces as characters. Pick @NotBlank for names and other text a person must actually type.

quiz.prompt: A controller method takes `@Valid @RequestBody CreateOrder body`, and the body breaks two constraints. What happens?
choices: Spring refuses it with 400 before the handler
The method runs with body.errors() filled in
Only the first violation is reported, as a 422
Spring drops the invalid fields and goes on
quiz.explanation: Spring validates the bound body before calling the method and throws MethodArgumentNotValidException, which the default handling turns into a 400. Both violations are collected, not only the first, and the method never runs with a half-valid object. Fields are never dropped silently, and the default status is 400, not 422.

quiz.prompt: `CreateOrder` holds `Address shipTo` without `@Valid`; `Address.city` is `@NotBlank`. A request has `"city": ""`. What does validating `CreateOrder` report?
choices: shipTo.city: must not be blank
A violation on shipTo itself
Nothing: Address is not validated
An error, because Address needs @Validated
quiz.explanation: Validation does not cascade into a nested object unless the reference is marked @Valid, so the blank city is never looked at and no path is reported. @Validated is for Spring proxies and groups, not for cascading. Mark the component @Valid, and the violation appears with the path shipTo.city.

quiz.prompt: A bean is annotated `@Validated`; its public `register(@Email String email)` is called as `this.register(...)` from another method of the same bean. Is the email checked?
choices: Yes, the annotation is on the method
Only when assertions are enabled
Yes, but the violation is only logged
No: the call skips the validating proxy
quiz.explanation: Method validation is applied by a proxy around the bean, and a call on this goes straight to the target object, so no check runs at all. It is the same trap as @Transactional and @PreAuthorize. Assertions and logging play no part; call through another bean, or validate at the edge.

quiz.prompt: A DTO declares `@NotNull int quantity`, and the client omits quantity. What does the server see?
choices: quantity is 0 and passes
A NotNull violation for quantity
A JSON parse error
quantity is null in the DTO
quiz.explanation: A primitive cannot be null, so the missing value binds to 0 and @NotNull has nothing to refuse. The JSON is valid and no parse error occurs. Use Integer with @NotNull when sending the field is required, or @Min(1) when zero is not a legal quantity, so the bad request is caught.

quiz.prompt: You write a `@PostalCode` constraint. What should its `ConstraintValidator.isValid` return for `null`?
choices: false, since null is not a postal code
true, and leave required to @NotNull
It should throw IllegalArgumentException
